The weight acts at mid-width, so its lever arm about the front edge is half the width.

A.statement: A loaded dump truck is traveling at $50\text{ mph}$ on a level haul road when the driver brakes. The truck slows at a constant $10\text{ ft/sec}^2$. How far does it travel from the moment the brakes take hold until it stops?
choiceNotes: Converts mph to ft/sec upside down (multiplies by 3,600/5,280), so the speed comes out as 34.1 ft/sec instead of 73.3 ft/sec and $34.1^2/20 = 58\text{ ft}$.
Leaves the speed in mph: $50^2/(2 \times 10) = 125$. The units do not match the ft/sec^2 deceleration.
Drops the 2 in $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2as$, or multiplies the starting speed by the stopping time instead of using the average speed. Both double the answer to $538\text{ ft}$.
A.eli5: First turn the speed into feet per second so it matches the braking rate. Then use the one constant-acceleration equation that has no time in it: the speed squared, divided by twice the braking rate, is how far the truck rolls.
A.hint: Convert 50 mph to ft/sec first. Which constant-acceleration equation links speed and distance without time?

steps.text: Convert the speed: 1 mph is 5,280 ft per 3,600 s.
Constant deceleration from $v_0$ to rest. Use $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a(s - s_0)$ with $v = 0$ and $a = -10\text{ ft/sec}^2$.
Solve for the distance.
Check with time: the truck stops in $73.3/10 = 7.33\text{ s}$ at an average speed of $36.7\text{ ft/sec}$, and $36.7 \times 7.33 = 269\text{ ft}$.

traps: Mph must become ft/sec before it meets ft/sec^2: multiply by 5,280/3,600 (about 1.467), not the other way round.
The 2 in $2as$ is easy to drop and doubles the distance.
Distance during braking uses the average speed, not the starting speed, times the time.

A.statement: A delivery van takes a flat freeway exit loop of radius $80\text{ m}$ at $15\text{ m/s}$. Its tires can supply a total horizontal acceleration of at most $0.40g$ before skidding. At that speed on the loop, what is the largest rate at which the driver can slow the van along its path without skidding? Use $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$.
choiceNotes: Subtracts the normal acceleration from the limit as plain numbers. The two parts are perpendicular, so their squares subtract, not the values.
Correct: $a_n = 15^2/80 = 2.81\text{ m/s}^2$ is already used up by turning, leaving $a_t = \sqrt{3.92^2 - 2.81^2} = 2.74\text{ m/s}^2$ for braking.
Uses the whole $0.40g$ for braking, as if the van were on a straight road. Turning already takes part of the tires' grip.
Adds the squares instead of subtracting: $\sqrt{3.92^2 + 2.81^2}$. The braking part must be smaller than the total, not larger.
A.eli5: The tires can only push so hard in total. Going around the loop already uses some of that push to turn the van toward the center. Turning and braking pull at right angles, so the total is the long side of a right triangle: whatever is left over on the other side is what you can use to slow down.
A.hint: Find the normal part $v^2/\rho$. The total acceleration is the hypotenuse of the normal and tangential parts.

steps.text: Largest total acceleration the tires can give.
Normal (centripetal) part needed just to follow the loop at 15 m/s.
Normal and tangential parts are perpendicular, so $a^2 = a_n^2 + a_t^2$. Solve for the tangential (braking) part.

traps: A vehicle on a curve accelerates toward the center even at constant speed; braking adds a second, perpendicular part.
Perpendicular components combine as squares: $a^2 = a_n^2 + a_t^2$. Never add or subtract the values directly.
The limit $0.40g$ must be turned into m/s^2 before it is compared with $v^2/\rho$.

A.statement: Gravel leaves the head of an inclined conveyor at $4.0\text{ m/s}$, moving $20\degree$ above the horizontal, from a point $6.0\text{ m}$ above level ground (see figure). Ignoring air resistance and using $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$, what horizontal distance $x$ from the discharge point does the gravel land?
choiceNotes: Swaps sine and cosine: uses $4.0\sin 20\degree$ as the horizontal speed and $4.0\cos 20\degree$ as the upward speed.
Takes the initial vertical speed as downward, so the gravel loses its small rise and lands too soon ($t = 0.98\text{ s}$).
Treats the launch as horizontal at the full $4.0\text{ m/s}$: $t = \sqrt{2(6)/9.81} = 1.11\text{ s}$, $x = 4.0 \times 1.11$.
Correct: the flight lasts $1.254\text{ s}$ and the horizontal speed is $3.76\text{ m/s}$, so $x = 4.71\text{ m}$.
A.eli5: Split the launch speed into a sideways part and an upward part. The upward part plus gravity decides how long the gravel is in the air before it drops 6 m. During that whole time it drifts sideways at a steady speed, so distance is sideways speed times time.
A.hint: Write $y(t)$ with the ground 6.0 m below the start and solve the quadratic for the positive time.

steps.text: Components of the launch velocity.
Vertical position with the discharge point as the origin, up positive. The gravel lands at $y = -6.0\text{ m}$.
Rearrange and take the positive root.
Horizontal motion has no acceleration.

A.handbookFormula: x = v_0\cos(\theta)\,t + x_0,\quad y = -gt^2/2 + v_0\sin(\theta)\,t + y_0
traps: Horizontal speed uses the cosine of the angle measured from the horizontal; vertical uses the sine.
The start is above the ground: the landing height is $-6.0\text{ m}$, not 0, so the time does not come from the symmetric range formula.
Keep the sign of the initial vertical speed: here it points up, which lengthens the flight.

A.statement: A railroad crossing gate arm is modeled as a uniform slender rod $6.0\text{ m}$ long with a mass of $18\text{ kg}$. It rotates about a horizontal pin $O$ located $0.5\text{ m}$ from one end (see figure). What is the arm's mass moment of inertia about the pin?
choiceNotes: Starts from the end value $mL^2/3$ and subtracts $m(0.5)^2$. The parallel-axis theorem only works from the centroidal axis, never from one non-centroidal axis to another.
Uses $mL^2/3$, the value about the end of the rod. The pin is 0.5 m in from the end, not at it.
Adds the pin offset to the half-length ($d = 3.0 + 0.5 = 3.5\text{ m}$). The pin is between the end and the center, so the distance is $3.0 - 0.5$.
A.eli5: The book gives the moment of inertia of a rod about its middle. To move to another parallel axis, add the mass times the square of how far that axis is from the middle. The middle of a 6 m rod is 3 m from the end, so the pin is 2.5 m from it.
A.hint: Where is the rod's center of mass, and how far is it from the pin?

steps.text: Centroidal moment of inertia of a slender rod about an axis perpendicular to it.
The center of mass is at mid-length, 3.0 m from either end, so its distance from the pin is:
Parallel-axis theorem.

traps: The transfer distance in $I_c + md^2$ is from the center of mass to the new axis, not from the end of the rod.
You may only transfer from the centroidal axis; going end-to-pin with $md^2$ gives a wrong answer.
$mL^2/3$ applies only to an axis exactly at the end of the rod.

A.statement: A $25\text{ kg}$ crate A rests on a level deck where the coefficient of kinetic friction is $0.20$. A light cord runs from the crate over a frictionless pulley at the deck edge to a hanging $15\text{ kg}$ bucket B (see figure). The system is released from rest and moves. Using $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$, what is the tension in the cord while it moves?
choiceNotes: Ignores the friction on the crate: $a = 3.68\text{ m/s}^2$ and $T = 25 \times 3.68 = 92.0\text{ N}$.
Sets the tension equal to the bucket's weight. That is only true if nothing accelerates; a falling bucket pulls with less than its weight.
Gets the sign of the bucket's acceleration wrong: $T = m_B(g + a)$ would be the tension if the bucket were accelerating upward.
A.eli5: The bucket's weight pulls the whole pair, the crate's friction holds it back, and what is left speeds up both masses together. Once you know how fast they speed up, the cord pulls on the bucket with less than its weight, because some of that weight goes into making the bucket fall faster.
A.hint: Find the common acceleration of the two bodies first, then write $\Sigma F = ma$ for the bucket alone.

steps.text: Friction on the crate (normal force equals its weight on a level deck).
Treat both bodies together: the bucket's weight minus friction accelerates the total mass.
Free body of the bucket, down positive.
steps.latex: m_B g - T = m_B a \;\Rightarrow\; T = 15(9.81 - 2.45) = 110\text{ N}

steps.text: Check with the crate: $T - F_f = m_A a$ gives $T = 25(2.45) + 49.05 = 110\text{ N}$.

traps: The tension is not the hanging weight once the system accelerates.
Friction acts only on the crate on the deck, and uses the crate's normal force, not the total mass.
Both bodies share one acceleration because the cord does not stretch.

A.statement: A hoist drum of radius $0.25\text{ m}$ turns on a frictionless axle and has a mass moment of inertia of $12\text{ kg}{\cdot}\text{m}^2$ about it. A $50\text{ kg}$ load hangs from a light rope wrapped around the drum (see figure). The brake is released and the load falls from rest. Using $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$, what is the angular acceleration of the drum?
choiceNotes: This is the load's linear acceleration $a = \alpha r$ in m/s^2, not the drum's angular acceleration.
Correct: $\alpha = m g r/(I + m r^2) = 122.6/15.125 = 8.11\text{ rad/s}^2$.
Assumes the rope tension equals the load's weight, $\alpha = mgr/I$. A falling load pulls with less than its weight.
Assumes the load falls freely at $g$, so $\alpha = g/r$. That ignores the drum's inertia completely.
A.eli5: The falling load spins the drum, but the drum resists being spun up, so the load falls slower than free fall and the rope pulls with less than the load's weight. Write one equation for the load, one for the drum, tie them together with $a = \alpha r$, and solve.
A.hint: Write $\Sigma F = ma$ for the load and $\Sigma M = I\alpha$ for the drum, then use $a = \alpha r$.

steps.text: Load, down positive.
Drum about its fixed axle.
The rope does not slip, so $a = \alpha r$. Substitute $T = mg - m\alpha r$ into the drum equation.
steps.latex: (mg - m\alpha r)\,r = I\alpha \;\Rightarrow\; \alpha = \frac{m g r}{I + m r^2}

steps.text: Put in the numbers.

traps: The rope tension is less than the load's weight while the load accelerates downward.
The answer asked for is angular (rad/s^2); $a = \alpha r$ in m/s^2 is a different quantity.
The load's own inertia ($m r^2$) adds to the drum's in the denominator.

A.statement: An aggregate plant conveyor raises $180$ metric tons of crushed stone per hour through a vertical rise of $12\text{ m}$. The drive system is $85\%$ efficient. Neglecting the kinetic energy of the stone, what input power must the drive receive?
choiceNotes: Leaves out $g$, treating kilograms per second as newtons: $50 \times 12/0.85 = 706\text{ W}$.
Multiplies by the efficiency instead of dividing. The input is always larger than the useful output.
This is the useful output power, before the 85% efficiency is accounted for.
Correct: output $= 50(9.81)(12) = 5.89\text{ kW}$, and input $= 5.89/0.85 = 6.92\text{ kW}$.
A.eli5: Power is how fast you lift weight up a height. Turn tons per hour into kilograms per second, multiply by $g$ to get newtons, then by the height. That is what the stone needs. The drive wastes 15%, so it has to take in more than that.
A.hint: Useful power is $\dot{m} g h$. Efficiency is output divided by input.

steps.text: Mass flow rate in kg/s.
Useful (output) power: the rate of gaining potential energy.
Input power from the efficiency.

traps: Divide by efficiency to go from output to input; multiplying makes the input smaller than the output.
A mass rate in kg/s must be multiplied by $g$ to become a weight rate in N/s.
A metric ton is 1,000 kg, and an hour is 3,600 s.

A.statement: A $3{,}000\text{ kg}$ drop hammer falls freely $1.5\text{ m}$ onto the cap of a steel pile and comes to rest without rebounding. The impact lasts $0.020\text{ s}$. Neglecting the hammer's weight during the short impact, what average force does the hammer exert on the pile? Use $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$.
choiceNotes: Correct: impact speed $\sqrt{2(9.81)(1.5)} = 5.42\text{ m/s}$, so $F = mv/\Delta t = 3{,}000(5.42)/0.020 = 814\text{ kN}$.
Doubles the change in velocity as if the hammer bounced back at the same speed. It stops, so the change is just $v$.
Divides the drop energy $mgh$ by the impact time. Energy over time is power, not force; impulse comes from momentum.
Uses $v = 2gh = 29.4$ and forgets the square root, which badly overstates the impact speed.
A.eli5: First find how fast the hammer is going when it hits: it falls 1.5 m. The pile has to take away all that momentum (mass times speed) in a fiftieth of a second. Force is momentum lost divided by the time it takes.
A.hint: Find the impact speed from free fall, then use impulse equals change in momentum.

steps.text: Impact speed after a free fall of $h = 1.5\text{ m}$.
Change in momentum: the hammer goes from $5.42\text{ m/s}$ to rest.
Impulse equals change in momentum, so the average force is:

traps: Impact speed is $\sqrt{2gh}$; forgetting the root gives a number in the wrong units and far too big.
Force over a time comes from momentum (impulse), not from energy.
With no rebound the velocity change is $v$, not $2v$.

B.statement: A construction personnel hoist on a high-rise site starts from rest at ground level and must stop at a deck $120\text{ ft}$ higher. It speeds up at a constant $4\text{ ft/sec}^2$ to its top speed of $16\text{ ft/sec}$, runs at that speed, then slows at a constant $4\text{ ft/sec}^2$ to stop exactly at the deck. How long does the trip take?
choiceNotes: Divides the whole rise by the top speed, as if the hoist were at $16\text{ ft/sec}$ the entire way. It ignores the time lost speeding up and slowing down.

Assumes the hoist speeds up the whole first half and slows the whole second half with no cruise: $2\sqrt{120/4} = 11.0\text{ sec}$. That would need a top speed of about $22\text{ ft/sec}$, above the hoist's $16\text{ ft/sec}$ limit.
Correct: $4\text{ sec}$ speeding up ($32\text{ ft}$), $3.5\text{ sec}$ cruising ($56\text{ ft}$) and $4\text{ sec}$ slowing ($32\text{ ft}$).
Adds the $4\text{ sec}$ speed-up and $4\text{ sec}$ slow-down to $120/16 = 7.5\text{ sec}$ of cruising, so the $64\text{ ft}$ covered while changing speed is counted twice.
B.eli5: Split the ride into three parts: speeding up, cruising and slowing down. Speeding up to 16 ft/sec at 4 ft/sec each second takes 4 seconds and covers 32 feet; slowing down is the mirror image. That leaves 56 feet to cruise at 16 ft/sec, which takes 3.5 seconds. Add the three times.
B.hint: Find the time and distance to reach top speed first. Only the leftover distance is covered at top speed.

steps.text: Speed-up phase from rest to $16\text{ ft/sec}$ at $4\text{ ft/sec}^2$.
The slow-down phase uses the same rate, so it is the mirror image.
Cruise over the remaining distance at top speed.
Add the three phases.

traps: Top speed is reached only after a speed-up distance; the hoist does not cover the whole rise at top speed.
Check that a no-cruise (speed up, then slow down) profile does not break the speed limit before using it.
Do not count the speed-up and slow-down distances again inside the cruise distance.

B.statement: A cable winch on a bridge erection barge has a drum $0.50\text{ m}$ in diameter. Starting from rest, the drum speeds up with constant angular acceleration and reaches $90\text{ rpm}$ after $4.0\text{ s}$. How much cable does the drum wind in during those $4.0\text{ s}$? Neglect the change in drum radius as cable layers build up.
choiceNotes: Finds the angle as $3$ revolutions but multiplies revolutions by the radius, leaving out the $2\pi$ that turns revolutions into radians.
Correct: $\omega = 9.42\text{ rad/s}$, $\theta = \tfrac{1}{2}\omega t = 18.85\text{ rad}$, and $s = r\theta = 0.25(18.85) = 4.71\text{ m}$.
Either multiplies the angle by the diameter instead of the radius, or uses $\theta = \omega t$ as if the drum turned at full speed the whole time. Both double the answer.
Treats $90\text{ rpm}$ as $90\text{ rad/s}$: $\tfrac{1}{2}(90)(4.0)(0.25) = 45\text{ m}$. Rpm must be converted before use.
B.eli5: The drum starts still and ends at 90 turns a minute, so on average it turns at 45 turns a minute. In 4 seconds that is 3 full turns. Each turn winds in one drum circumference, which is pi times 0.50 m. Three of those is 4.71 m.
B.hint: Convert rpm to rad/s. With constant angular acceleration from rest, the angle turned is half the final angular speed times the time. Cable length is radius times angle in radians.

steps.text: Convert the final speed to rad/s.
Constant angular acceleration from rest.
Angle turned in $4.0\text{ s}$.
Cable wound in is the arc length at the drum surface, radius $0.25\text{ m}$.

traps: Rpm is revolutions per minute: multiply by $2\pi/60$ to get rad/s.
Arc length $s = r\theta$ uses the radius and an angle in radians, not the diameter or revolutions.
Starting from rest the drum averages half its final speed, so the angle is $\tfrac{1}{2}\omega t$, not $\omega t$.

B.statement: A track inspection cart moves along a straight rail line. Its position is $s(t) = t^3 - 9t^2 + 24t$, where $s$ is in feet and $t$ is in seconds. What total distance does the cart travel between $t = 0$ and $t = 5\text{ sec}$?
choiceNotes: This is the displacement, $s(5) - s(0) = 20\text{ ft}$. The cart backs up between $t = 2$ and $t = 4\text{ sec}$, so distance and displacement differ.
Adds only the forward legs (20 ft and 4 ft) and drops the 4 ft the cart rolls backward. Backward travel still counts toward distance.
Correct: the cart turns around at $t = 2$ and $t = 4\text{ sec}$, so the distance is $20 + 4 + 4 = 28\text{ ft}$.
Adds the positions at $t = 2$, $4$ and $5\text{ sec}$ ($20 + 16 + 20$) instead of the changes in position between them.
B.eli5: Distance is how far the wheels roll, whichever way they go. Find when the cart stops and turns around (where its speed is zero), then add up the length of each leg as a positive number.
B.hint: Set $v = ds/dt = 0$ to find when the cart reverses. Add the absolute value of each leg.

steps.text: Velocity is the derivative of position.
The cart stops and reverses at $t = 2$ and $t = 4\text{ sec}$. Find the position at each turn and at the end.
steps.latex: s(0) = 0,\quad s(2) = 20\text{ ft},\quad s(4) = 16\text{ ft},\quad s(5) = 20\text{ ft}

steps.text: Add the leg lengths as positive numbers.

traps: Displacement (end minus start) is not distance when the motion reverses.
Find every time where $v = 0$ inside the interval; each one can start a new leg.
Add changes in position, not the positions themselves.

B.statement: A steel access hatch over a utility vault is a thin, uniform circular plate $0.80\text{ m}$ in diameter that weighs $1{,}177\text{ N}$. It swings open about a hinge line that lies in the plane of the plate and is tangent to its rim (see the plan view). What is the mass moment of inertia of the hatch about the hinge line? Use $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$.
choiceNotes: This is $\tfrac{1}{4}MR^2$, about a diameter through the center. The hinge is $R$ away from the center, so the parallel-axis term $MR^2$ is missing.
Uses $\tfrac{3}{2}MR^2$ from the handbook table. That axis is perpendicular to the plate through the rim, not in the plate's plane like this hinge.
Uses the weight in newtons as if it were the mass in kilograms, so the answer is $9.81$ times too large.
B.eli5: The hatch spins about its edge, not its middle, so it is harder to swing. Start with the handbook value for a thin disk turning about a line through its center lying in the plate (one quarter of mass times radius squared). Then slide that axis out to the edge by adding mass times the distance squared. Remember to turn the weight into a mass first.
B.hint: Pick the handbook axis that lies in the plate (not the one perpendicular to it), then use the parallel-axis theorem with $d = R$.

steps.text: Mass from the weight.
Thin circular disk, axis along a diameter (in the plane of the plate), $R = 0.40\text{ m}$.
The hinge line is parallel to that diameter and a distance $R$ from it.

traps: A weight in newtons must be divided by $g$ before it goes into a mass moment of inertia.
A thin disk has different inertias about a diameter ($\tfrac{1}{4}MR^2$) and about the axis perpendicular to it ($\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$). Pick the one parallel to the hinge.
The parallel-axis theorem starts from the centroidal axis; the distance here is the radius, not the diameter.

B.statement: A crane is lowering a precast concrete wall panel that weighs $30\text{ kN}$ at a steady $1.2\text{ m/s}$. The operator then brings the panel to a stop with a constant deceleration over $2.0\text{ s}$. What is the tension in the hoist cable while the panel is stopping? Use $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$.
choiceNotes: This is only the $ma$ term, the extra force needed to stop the panel. The cable also has to carry the panel's weight.
Subtracts $ma$ from the weight because the panel is moving down. Slowing a downward motion means the acceleration points up, so the cable pulls harder, not less.
The static tension. It holds only while the panel moves at constant speed, not while it is slowing.
B.eli5: The panel is going down and the operator is stopping it, so the cable must push back against that downward motion. That means the cable pulls more than the panel weighs, just as you feel heavier when an elevator going down comes to a stop.
B.hint: Which way does the acceleration point when a downward-moving load slows down? Convert the weight to a mass for the $ma$ term.

steps.text: Deceleration of the downward motion, which is an upward acceleration.
Mass of the panel from its weight.
Newton's second law, taking up as positive.

traps: Decelerating while moving down is an upward acceleration: the tension is above the weight.
A weight in kN is not a mass; divide by $g$ before multiplying by the acceleration.
Constant-speed tension equals the weight only when the acceleration is zero.

B.statement: A $40\text{ kg}$ crate of fittings is sliding up a loading ramp inclined at $20\degree$, pulled by a rope with a tension of $300\text{ N}$. The rope is held at $15\degree$ above the ramp surface (see figure). The coefficient of kinetic friction between the crate and the ramp is $0.25$. Using $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$, what is the acceleration of the crate up the ramp?
choiceNotes: Takes the normal force as $mg\cos 20\degree$ and forgets that the rope's upward component lifts the crate off the ramp, so the friction comes out too large ($92.2\text{ N}$ instead of $72.8\text{ N}$).
Leaves out friction entirely: $(289.8 - 134.2)/40 = 3.89\text{ m/s}^2$.
Leaves out the weight component along the ramp, $mg\sin 20\degree = 134.2\text{ N}$, as if the ramp were level.
B.eli5: Tilt your axes so one runs along the ramp. Across the ramp, the ramp pushes back with the part of the weight pressing into it, minus what the rope lifts. Friction is 0.25 times that push. Along the ramp, the rope pulls up while gravity and friction pull down. What is left over, divided by the mass, is the acceleration.
B.hint: Use axes along and perpendicular to the ramp. The rope has a component perpendicular to the ramp that changes the normal force.

steps.text: Weight and its components with axes along and perpendicular to the ramp.
steps.latex: mg = 40(9.81) = 392.4\text{ N},\quad mg\cos 20\degree = 368.7\text{ N},\quad mg\sin 20\degree = 134.2\text{ N}

steps.text: Rope components relative to the ramp.
No motion perpendicular to the ramp, so the forces there balance.
Kinetic friction acts down the ramp, against the motion.
Newton's second law along the ramp.

traps: A rope pulled at an angle above the surface reduces the normal force, and so the friction.
On a ramp, part of the weight acts down the slope and must be overcome as well as friction.
The rope angle here is measured from the ramp, not from the horizontal.

B.statement: A demolition wrecking ball that weighs $9.0\text{ kN}$ hangs from a cable whose length from the boom-tip pin to the center of the ball is $8.0\text{ m}$. The ball is pulled back until the cable makes $40\degree$ with the vertical and released from rest (see figure). Treating the ball as a particle and the cable as light, what is the cable tension as the ball swings through its lowest point?
choiceNotes: Subtracts $mv^2/L$ from the weight. At the bottom the ball's acceleration points up toward the pin, so the cable must pull harder than the weight.
This is $W\cos 40\degree$, the tension at the instant of release when the ball is not yet moving, not at the bottom of the swing.
The static tension. It ignores that the ball is moving on a circle at the bottom and needs a net upward force.
B.eli5: First find how fast the ball is going at the bottom: it drops by the cable length minus the cable length times the cosine of 40 degrees. Then remember the ball is swinging on a circle, so the cable has to hold up its weight and also pull it toward the pin to keep it turning. That makes the tension bigger than the weight.
B.hint: Energy gives the speed at the bottom from the height drop $L(1 - \cos\theta)$. Then use $\Sigma F_n = mv^2/L$ toward the pin.

steps.text: Height the ball drops from release to the lowest point.
Conservation of energy from rest (the tension does no work, it is always perpendicular to the path).
Mass of the ball.
At the bottom the acceleration is $v^2/L$ upward, toward the pin.

B.handbookFormula: T_2 + V_2 = T_1 + V_1,\quad F_n = m\frac{v_t^2}{\rho}
traps: The height drop is $L(1 - \cos\theta)$, not $L\sin\theta$ or $L\cos\theta$.
At the bottom of a swing the tension exceeds the weight; the centripetal term adds, it does not subtract.
Divide the weight by $g$ to get the mass used in $mv^2/L$.

B.statement: In a rail yard, a $30{,}000\text{ kg}$ freight car rolling at $2.0\text{ m/s}$ runs into a stationary $20{,}000\text{ kg}$ car on a level track, and the two couple together. Neglecting rolling resistance, how much kinetic energy is lost in the coupling?
choiceNotes: Correct: the coupled cars move at $60{,}000/50{,}000 = 1.2\text{ m/s}$, so the energy drops from $60\text{ kJ}$ to $36\text{ kJ}$, a loss of $24\text{ kJ}$.
This is the kinetic energy left after coupling, not the energy lost.
Drops the $\tfrac{1}{2}$ in kinetic energy, so both energies (and their difference) come out twice as large.
Assumes the whole $60\text{ kJ}$ is lost, as if the cars stopped. Momentum is conserved, so the coupled cars keep rolling.
B.eli5: When the cars lock together, momentum (mass times speed) stays the same, but now it is shared by more mass, so they roll slower. Kinetic energy is not kept in a collision where things stick together. Find the energy before and after; the difference went into the couplers, noise and heat.
B.hint: Use conservation of momentum to find the common speed, then compare kinetic energy before and after.

steps.text: Momentum is conserved in the impact (perfectly plastic, $e = 0$).
Kinetic energy before the coupling.
Kinetic energy after the coupling.
Energy lost.

traps: In an impact momentum is always conserved; kinetic energy is conserved only when $e = 1$.
Coupled cars keep moving at a shared speed; they do not stop.
Asked for the energy lost, give the difference, not the energy that remains.

A.statement: The shear diagram shown belongs to a beam with a pin at A, a roller at B, and an overhang ending at the free end C. The bending moment at support B (kip-ft) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Takes only the area of the negative segment between the load point and B and forgets the positive area from A.
Correct: M at A is zero (pin), and adding the signed shear areas from A to B gives 33 - 57 = -24 kip-ft.
Stops at the first segment: 33 kip-ft is the moment under the point where the shear changes sign, not at B.
Adds the two areas as positive numbers, ignoring that the second one is negative.
A.eli5: The moment at any point equals the moment at the start plus the area under the shear diagram up to that point. At the pin A the moment is zero. From A the shear is +5.5 kips for 6 ft (area +33), then -9.5 kips for 6 ft (area -57). So at B the moment is 0 + 33 - 57 = -24 kip-ft. The overhang lets you check: the last 4 ft has area +24, which brings the moment back to zero at the free end C.
A.hint: Start at A with M = 0 and add the shear areas, keeping their signs.

steps.text: At the pin A the bending moment is zero.
Area under the shear diagram from A to the load point (6 ft at +5.5 kips).
Area from the load point to B (6 ft at -9.5 kips).
Moment at B is the running sum.
Check from the free end: the overhang area is (6.0)(4) = +24, and M_C must be zero.

traps: Adding shear areas without their signs.
Reporting the largest positive moment (under the load) when the question asks for the moment at the support.
Forgetting that the moment at a pin at the end of a beam is zero, so the running sum starts at zero.

A.statement: A simply supported beam carries only a clockwise concentrated couple $M_0$ applied one third of the span from the left support, as shown. With positive moment (concave up) drawn above the axis, which bending moment diagram is correct?
choiceNotes: A triangle with a peak and no jump is the shape for a concentrated force, not a couple.
Has the jump, but in the wrong direction: a clockwise couple makes the moment jump up (in the positive direction) moving left to right.
Shows a constant moment after the couple, which would need zero shear; here the reactions form a couple, so the shear is a nonzero constant and the moment must slope.
Correct: the reactions are equal and opposite, so the shear is constant (-M0/L) and both segments have the same slope; the moment falls to -M0/3, jumps up by M0 to +2M0/3, and returns to zero at B.
A.eli5: A couple twists the beam without pushing it up or down. To keep the beam still, the supports push one up and one down by the same amount, M0/L. So the shear is the same everywhere, which means the moment diagram is made of straight lines with the same slope. Where the couple sits, the moment jumps by exactly M0. A clockwise couple makes it jump up as you move right. Diagram IV is the only one with parallel slopes and an upward jump.
A.hint: Equal and opposite reactions mean constant shear. What does constant shear do to the slope of the moment diagram?

steps.text: Sum moments about A: the reactions form a couple that balances M0.
The shear is constant over the whole span, so the moment diagram has one constant slope.
Just left of the couple, at x = L/3:
A clockwise applied couple makes the moment jump by +M0, and the line returns to zero at B.

traps: Treating a couple like a point force and drawing a peak.
Getting the direction of the jump backwards.
Assuming the shear is zero because no vertical load is applied: the reactions still create shear.

A.statement: The stem of a cantilever retaining wall is 10 ft tall. A 1-ft-wide strip of the stem is treated as a vertical cantilever fixed at the footing, loaded by lateral earth pressure that rises linearly from zero at the top to $0.60$ kip/ft at the base, as shown. The bending moment at the base of the strip (kip-ft) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: This is the shear at the base (the resultant, w0 L / 2), not the moment.
Correct: resultant 3.0 kips acting at one third of the height above the base, so M = 3.0 x 10/3 = 10 kip-ft (w0 L^2 / 6).
Places the resultant at two thirds of the height above the base (the centroid measured from the wrong end).
Treats the load as uniform at 0.60 kip/ft over the full height (w L^2 / 2).
A.eli5: The soil pushes harder the deeper you go, so the load is a triangle. Replace the triangle by one force: its size is the triangle area, half of 0.60 times 10, which is 3 kips. That force acts at the centroid of the triangle, one third of the way up from the base, 3.33 ft. The moment at the base is 3 kips times 3.33 ft, 10 kip-ft.
A.hint: Replace the triangular load by its resultant and find where it acts.

steps.text: Resultant of the triangular load (area of the triangle).
It acts at the centroid, one third of the height above the base.
Moment at the fixed base.

traps: Using w L^2/2 as if the load were uniform.
Putting the triangle resultant at 2L/3 from the base instead of L/3.
Giving the shear (resultant force) instead of the moment.

A.topic: Stresses (axial, torsion, bending, transverse shear, thermal, thin-walled vessels)
A.statement: Two steel plates are joined end to end by a butt splice with a splice plate on each face, as shown. There is one $3/4$-in.-diameter bolt on each side of the joint, and the plates carry a tension of 18 kips. The average shear stress in a bolt (ksi) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Uses pi d^2 for the area (the diameter plugged into pi r^2), four times too much area.
Splits the load between both bolts as well as the two shear planes. Each bolt on its own side of the joint carries the full 18 kips.
Correct: each bolt is in double shear, so tau = P / (2A) = 18 / (2 x 0.442) = 20.4 ksi.
Treats the bolt as single shear, using one area.
A.eli5: All 18 kips must pass from the left plate into the splice plates through the one bolt on the left side. That bolt is pinched by two splice plates, one above and one below, so it would have to be cut in two places to fail. Two cut faces share the 18 kips, 9 kips each. Divide by the bolt area, 0.442 square inches, and you get about 20.4 ksi.
A.hint: Count the planes the bolt would have to shear through, and how many bolts carry the load on one side of the joint.

steps.text: Bolt area.
One bolt per side carries the full load through two shear planes (double shear).
Average shear stress.

traps: Single shear instead of double shear.
Dividing the load by both bolts when each one sits on its own side of the joint.
Using the diameter in place of the radius in pi r^2.

A.topic: Stresses (axial, torsion, bending, transverse shear, thermal, thin-walled vessels)
A.statement: An open-top steel water standpipe has a diameter of 30 ft and holds water 80 ft deep. The wall plate at the base is 0.50 in. thick. Using thin-wall theory, the hoop stress in the wall at the base (ksi) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Leaves the diameter in feet while the pressure is in psi and the thickness in inches.
This is pr/(2t), the longitudinal stress of a capped vessel. An open-top standpipe has no pressure-driven longitudinal stress, and in any case the hoop stress governs.
Uses the diameter in place of the radius in p r / t.
A.eli5: Water pushes out on the wall, harder at the bottom. At 80 ft deep the pressure is about 35 psi. That pressure tries to split the tank along a vertical line, and the wall resists with hoop stress, pressure times radius divided by thickness. The radius is 15 ft, or 180 in., so 34.7 times 180 divided by 0.5 is about 12,500 psi.
A.hint: Get the pressure at the base in psi first, then use the hoop stress formula with the radius in inches.

steps.text: Water pressure at the base, converted to psi.
Radius in inches.
Thin-wall hoop stress (t/r = 0.003, well under 0.1).

traps: Using the diameter instead of the radius.
Mixing feet and inches in p r / t.
Reporting the longitudinal stress (half the hoop stress).

A.topic: Stresses (axial, torsion, bending, transverse shear, thermal, thin-walled vessels)
A.statement: A highway sign is mounted on a single steel pipe post fixed at the ground. The pipe has an outside diameter of 6.625 in. and a wall thickness of 0.280 in. The wind resultant on the sign is 0.80 kip acting 10 ft above the base, as shown. The maximum bending stress in the post at the base (ksi) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Leaves the moment in kip-ft (8.0) while I and c are in inches.
Uses the moment of inertia of a solid 6.625-in. bar, ignoring the hole.
Uses the full outside diameter as c instead of half of it.
A.eli5: The wind pushes the sign sideways, and the post acts like a diving board standing on end. The bending moment at the ground is the force times its height: 0.8 kip times 10 ft is 8 kip-ft, or 96 kip-in. The pipe resists with its moment of inertia, which for a tube is the outer circle minus the hole. The outermost fiber is half the outside diameter from the center. Moment times that distance, divided by I, gives about 11.3 ksi.
A.hint: Moment in kip-in, I of a hollow circle, c = outside radius.

steps.text: Inside diameter.
Moment of inertia of the tube.
Moment at the base, in kip-in.
Maximum bending stress, c = outside radius.

traps: Using the solid-section I for a hollow pipe.
Using the diameter instead of the radius for c.
Leaving the moment in kip-ft.

A.topic: Stresses (axial, torsion, bending, transverse shear, thermal, thin-walled vessels)
A.statement: A timber T-beam is built from an 8 in. by 2 in. flange plank nailed to a 2 in. by 10 in. web plank, as shown (actual dimensions). One row of nails joins them, each nail good for 250 lb in shear. For a vertical shear of 600 lb, the maximum nail spacing along the beam (in.) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Divides the nail capacity by two, as if each nail had two shear planes to share.
Puts the neutral axis at mid-depth (6 in.) instead of at the centroid of the T.
Uses Q for everything above the neutral axis (flange plus part of the web). The nails only transfer the flange's share.
Correct: neutral axis 7.67 in. above the bottom, I = 492 in^4, Q of the flange = 16 x 3.33 = 53.3 in^3, q = 600 x 53.3 / 492 = 65.0 lb/in., s = 250 / 65.0 = 3.84 in.
A.eli5: When the beam bends, the flange wants to slide along the top of the web, and the nails stop it. The sliding force per inch of beam is the shear flow, V Q over I, where Q is the first moment of just the piece the nails hold on: the flange. Find the neutral axis of the T, then I, then Q of the flange about that axis. The shear flow comes out to 65 lb per inch, and a 250-lb nail can handle 250/65 = 3.8 in. of beam.
A.hint: The nails carry the shear flow at the flange-web joint, so Q is the flange area times its distance to the neutral axis.

steps.text: Neutral axis from the bottom of the web (flange centroid at 11 in., web centroid at 5 in.).
Moment of inertia about the neutral axis (parallel-axis theorem).
First moment of the flange about the neutral axis.
Shear flow at the joint.
Nail spacing.

traps: Taking Q at the neutral axis instead of at the joint.
Assuming the neutral axis is at mid-depth of an unsymmetric section.
Treating the nail as if it were in double shear.

A.topic: Deformations (axial, torsional twist, beam deflection, thermal)
A.statement: A 25-ft steel rod ($E = 29{,}000$ ksi, $\alpha = 6.5 \times 10^{-6}$/°F) is anchored to a rigid wall at one end. At installation there is a 0.040-in. gap between its other end and a rigid abutment, as shown. If the rod temperature then rises 90°F, the axial stress in the rod (ksi) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Correct: free expansion 6.5e-6 x 90 x 300 = 0.1755 in.; the gap absorbs 0.040 in.; the abutment prevents the other 0.1355 in., so sigma = E (0.1355 / 300) = 13.1 ksi (compression).
Ignores the gap and treats the rod as fully restrained (E alpha delta T).
Adds the gap to the free expansion instead of subtracting it.
Divides the prevented elongation in inches by the length in feet.
A.eli5: If nothing stopped it, the warm rod would grow 0.1755 in. The first 0.040 in. of growth is free, because it just closes the gap. After that the abutment stops the rod, so the wall has to push back hard enough to squeeze out the remaining 0.1355 in. Squeezing 0.1355 in. out of 300 in. of steel takes E times 0.1355/300, about 13.1 ksi.
A.hint: Only the expansion left over after the gap closes is resisted.

steps.text: Free thermal expansion over 300 in.
The gap takes 0.040 in.; the rest is prevented by the abutment.
Compatibility: the wall force must shorten the rod by that amount, PL/AE = 0.1355.

traps: Ignoring the gap.
Adding the gap instead of subtracting it.
Mixing feet and inches in the strain.

A.topic: Deformations (axial, torsional twist, beam deflection, thermal)
A.statement: A solid 50-mm steel shaft ($G = 80$ GPa) is fixed at A and carries the two torques shown, applied in opposite directions at B and at the free end C. The magnitude of the angle of twist at C relative to A (degrees) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Uses the moment of inertia I = pi d^4 / 64 instead of the polar moment J, which doubles the answer.
Applies the net 1.8 kN m over the whole 1.0 m, ignoring that segment BC carries a different torque.
Adds the two torques as if they acted in the same direction, so segment AB carries 4.2 kN m.
A.eli5: Each piece of the shaft twists by its own torque times its length over G J. Cut through BC and the only torque on the free piece is 1.2 kN m. Cut through AB and you get 1.2 minus 3.0, so 1.8 kN m the other way. The long piece twists one way, the short piece the other way, and they partly cancel: the net twist is 0.60 kN m^2 divided by G J, about 0.0122 rad, or 0.70 degrees.
A.hint: Find the internal torque in each segment, with signs, and add the twists.

steps.text: Polar moment of inertia.
Internal torques (cutting from the free end C).
Sum the segment twists.
Convert to degrees.

traps: Using I instead of J.
Using one torque over the whole length instead of segment by segment.
Losing the sign of the torques so the twists add instead of partly cancelling.

A.topic: Deformations (axial, torsional twist, beam deflection, thermal)
A.statement: Floor joists of Douglas fir ($E = 1{,}600$ ksi) are spaced 16 in. on center and span 15 ft, simply supported. Each joist has $I = 98.9\ \text{in}^4$, and the floor live load is 40 psf. The midspan live-load deflection of a joist (in.) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Takes the joist load as 40 lb/ft, ignoring that each joist carries a 16-in. (1.33-ft) tributary width.
Uses the point-load coefficient 1/48 with the total load wL instead of 5/384 for a uniform load.
Keeps w in lb/ft while L is in inches, which makes the answer 12 times too large.
A.eli5: Each joist holds up a strip of floor 16 in. wide, so it carries 40 psf times 1.33 ft, about 53 lb per foot of joist. For a simply supported beam with a uniform load, the middle sags 5 w L^4 over 384 E I. Put every number in pounds and inches (w = 4.44 lb/in., L = 180 in., E = 1,600,000 psi) and the sag is about 0.38 in.
A.hint: Turn the floor load into a load per inch of joist using the spacing, and keep all units in pounds and inches.

steps.text: Load per joist from the tributary width.
Span in inches and E in psi.
Midspan deflection for a uniform load.

traps: Forgetting the tributary width (spacing) of the joist.
Leaving w in lb/ft with L in inches.
Using the point-load formula for a distributed load.

A.topic: Combined stresses, principal stresses, Mohr's circle
A.statement: A short concrete pedestal 16 in. by 24 in. in plan carries a compressive load of 120 kips applied 4 in. off center along the 24-in. direction, as shown. The maximum compressive stress on the base of the pedestal (psi) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: This is the stress on the opposite edge: the load sits at the edge of the kern (e = h/6), so the minimum stress is exactly zero.
This is P/A alone; it leaves out the bending from the eccentricity.
Uses the full 24-in. depth as c instead of half of it, doubling the bending part.
A.eli5: An off-center load does two things at once: it squeezes the whole base evenly (P/A), and it tips the pedestal toward the load side, adding squeeze on that side and taking it away on the other (M/S). Here both parts happen to be 312.5 psi. On the side nearer the load they add to 625 psi; on the far side they cancel to zero.
A.hint: Add the uniform part P/A and the bending part Mc/I, with M = P e and bending about the axis parallel to the 16-in. side.

steps.text: Area and the section modulus about the axis parallel to the 16-in. side (depth 24 in. in the direction of e).
Moment from the eccentricity.
Combine axial and bending stress on the face nearer the load.

traps: Forgetting the bending part of an eccentric load.
Bending about the wrong axis (using 24 x 16^2 / 6).
Using the full depth instead of c = h/2.

A.topic: Combined stresses, principal stresses, Mohr's circle
A.statement: The plane stress element shown is taken from the web of a loaded steel girder. The maximum in-plane shear stress at this point (MPa) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: This is the center of Mohr's circle, (sigma_x + sigma_y)/2, the average normal stress.
Drops the minus sign on the compressive sigma_x: (45 - 75)/2 = -15, so R = sqrt(15^2 + 32^2) = 35 MPa.
Uses (sigma_x - sigma_y)/2 and leaves out the shear stress term.
A.eli5: Draw Mohr's circle. The two faces give the points (-45, 32) and (75, -32). The center is halfway between them, at 15 MPa. The radius is the distance from the center to either point: 60 across and 32 up, so the square root of 60^2 + 32^2, which is 68. The biggest in-plane shear stress is always the radius.
A.hint: The maximum in-plane shear stress is the radius of Mohr's circle. Watch the sign of the compressive stress.

steps.text: Read the element: sigma_x is compressive, sigma_y tensile.
Half the difference of the normal stresses.
Radius of Mohr's circle = maximum in-plane shear stress.

traps: Dropping the minus sign on the compressive stress, which gives (45 - 75)/2 = -15 and R = 35.
Leaving out the shear term.
Reporting a principal stress instead of the radius.

A.topic: Combined stresses, principal stresses, Mohr's circle
A.statement: A closed-end steel pipe with a mean diameter of 600 mm and a wall thickness of 8 mm carries an internal pressure of 1.6 MPa and, at the same time, a torque of 60 kN·m, as shown. The maximum principal stress in the wall, away from the ends (MPa), is most nearly:
choiceNotes: This is the hoop stress alone; it ignores the axial stress and the torsional shear.
Correct: hoop 60 MPa, axial 30 MPa, torsional shear 13.3 MPa; sigma_1 = 45 + sqrt(15^2 + 13.3^2) = 65.0 MPa.
Adds the shear stress straight onto the hoop stress (60 + 13.3) instead of combining them on Mohr's circle.
Uses the 600-mm diameter as the radius, doubling both pressure stresses.
A.eli5: The pressure makes two stresses in the wall: around the pipe (hoop), 60 MPa, and along it (axial), half that, 30 MPa. The torque adds a shear stress of 13.3 MPa on the same element. Put those three on Mohr's circle: center 45, radius the square root of 15^2 + 13.3^2, which is 20. The largest normal stress is center plus radius, 65 MPa.
A.hint: Find the hoop, axial and torsional shear stresses on one wall element, then combine them with Mohr's circle.

steps.text: Hoop and axial stress, thin wall (r = 300 mm).
Torsional shear in a thin-walled tube, A_m = pi r^2.
Mohr's circle center and radius.
Maximum principal stress.

traps: Ignoring the axial stress from the end caps.
Adding shear and normal stress directly.
Using the diameter in place of the radius.

B.statement: A 20-ft simply supported floor beam carries a 10-kip concentrated load 5 ft from support A and a uniform load of 4 kip/ft over the right half of the span, as shown. Neglect the beam weight. The maximum bending moment in the beam (kip-ft) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Assumes the maximum moment is under the concentrated load. The shear is still positive there, so the moment keeps rising.
Takes the moment at the centroid of the uniform load (15 ft from A) instead of where the shear is zero.
Takes the moment at midspan, where the uniform load starts. The shear is still +7.5 kips there, so the moment has not peaked yet.
Correct: the shear reaches zero 11.875 ft from A, and the moment there is 132 kip-ft.
B.eli5: The biggest bending moment sits where the shear crosses zero. Find the left reaction first: 17.5 kips. Walking right, the shear is 17.5 kips, drops to 7.5 kips at the point load, and starts falling by 4 kips per foot once the uniform load begins at midspan. It reaches zero 7.5/4 = 1.875 ft past midspan. Add up the shear areas to that point and you get 132 kip-ft.
B.hint: Find where the shear diagram crosses zero; that is where the moment peaks.

steps.text: Sum moments about B to get the left reaction. The uniform load resultant is 40 kips acting 5 ft from B.
Shear just right of the point load, and where it goes to zero inside the uniform load (which starts at x = 10 ft).
Moment at midspan from the shear areas.
Add the triangle of shear from midspan to the zero-shear point.
Check from the right: R_B = 32.5 kips, and the zero-shear point is 8.125 ft from B.

traps: Stopping at the concentrated load or at midspan: the moment peaks where the shear changes sign, not at a load point here.
Placing the uniform load resultant at midspan instead of at the middle of the loaded half.

B.statement: The shear diagram shown is for a simply supported beam with a pin at A and a roller at C. The loads are not drawn. The concentrated load acting on the beam at point B (kips) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Reads the shear value just to the right of B instead of the size of the jump.
Correct: the shear jumps from +16 to +4 kips at B, a sudden drop of 12 kips, so a 12-kip downward load acts there.
Reads the shear just to the left of B, which is the left reaction, not the load at B.
Adds the two shear values at B (16 + 4) instead of taking their difference.
B.eli5: A concentrated load makes the shear diagram jump straight up or down by the size of the load. At B the diagram drops from +16 to +4 kips. The drop is 12 kips, so there is a 12-kip load pushing down at B. The sloped line after B is the uniform load, a separate thing.
B.hint: A vertical step in the shear diagram equals the concentrated load at that point.

steps.text: Read the shear just left and just right of B.
The jump equals the concentrated load; a drop means the load acts downward.
Check: the slope from B to C is (4 + 20)/12 = 2 kip/ft, a 24-kip uniform load. Total load 12 + 24 = 36 kips equals the reactions 16 + 20.

traps: Reading a single shear value instead of the size of the step.
Confusing the sloped part of the diagram (a distributed load) with a concentrated load.

B.topic: Stresses (axial, torsion, bending, transverse shear, thermal, thin-walled vessels)
B.statement: A continuous welded steel rail ($E = 29{,}000$ ksi, $\alpha = 6.5 \times 10^{-6}$/°F, cross-sectional area $13.0\ \text{in}^2$) is anchored so it cannot change length. It is stress-free at 85°F. On a winter night the rail temperature drops to -5°F. The axial force in the rail (kips) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Stops at the stress (17.0 ksi) and never multiplies by the rail area.
Uses a temperature change of 80°F by mishandling the negative final temperature (85 - 5 instead of 85 - (-5)).
Correct: a 90°F drop gives a thermal stress of 17.0 ksi in tension, and 17.0 times 13.0 square inches is about 221 kips.
Uses the SI coefficient (11.7 per million per °C) with a temperature change in °F.
B.eli5: Cooling steel wants to shrink. The anchors hold the rail at its original length, so the rail ends up stretched by exactly the amount it wanted to shrink. That pull is a stress of E times alpha times the temperature change, and the force is that stress times the area. The drop from 85°F to -5°F is 90°F, not 80°F.
B.hint: Fully restrained member: stress equals E times alpha times delta T. Then force equals stress times area.

steps.text: Temperature change.
Free thermal strain the anchors prevent.
Stress needed to cancel it (tension, since the rail wants to shorten).
Axial force in the rail.

traps: Subtracting a negative temperature wrongly: from 85°F to -5°F is a 90°F change.
Mixing the °C and °F values of the expansion coefficient.
Answering with a stress when the question asks for a force.

B.topic: Stresses (axial, torsion, bending, transverse shear, thermal, thin-walled vessels)
B.statement: A closed cylindrical compressed-air receiver at a construction yard has a mean diameter of 1.5 m and a wall thickness of 12 mm. The internal pressure is 1.2 MPa. Using thin-wall theory, the longitudinal (axial) stress in the shell away from the heads (MPa) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Divides by 4t while also using the radius, a mix of the pd/4t and pr/2t forms that halves the answer.
Correct: axial stress is pr/(2t) = 1.2(750)/(2 x 12) = 37.5 MPa.
Gives the hoop stress pr/t, or uses the diameter in pr/2t. Either error doubles the answer.
Uses the diameter in the hoop formula, pd/t, which is four times the axial stress.
B.eli5: Pressure pushes the two end caps apart, and the whole ring of steel around the tank resists that push. The steel ring is long (the circumference) and the pushed area is the circle, which works out to a stress of pressure times radius over twice the thickness. The hoop stress, which tries to split the tank along its length, is twice as large.
B.hint: For a thin cylinder, axial stress is half the hoop stress: pr over 2t.

steps.text: Mean radius in millimetres.
Thin-wall check: t/r = 12/750 = 0.016, well under 0.1.
Axial stress from the handbook thin-wall formula.

traps: Reporting the hoop stress (twice as large) when the question asks for the axial stress.
Using the diameter where the formula has the radius.

B.topic: Stresses (axial, torsion, bending, transverse shear, thermal, thin-walled vessels)
B.statement: A hollow steel shaft that drives a sluice gate hoist has an outside diameter of 3.0 in. and an inside diameter of 2.0 in. It carries a torque of 30 kip-in., as shown. The shear stress at the inside surface of the shaft (ksi) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Correct: J = 6.38 in.^4 for the hollow section, and at the inside surface r = 1.0 in., so the stress is 30(1.0)/6.38 = 4.70 ksi.
Uses the outside radius (1.5 in.), which gives the maximum stress at the outer surface, not the stress at the inside surface.
Uses the inside diameter (2.0 in.) as the radius.
Uses the outside diameter (3.0 in.) as the radius.
B.eli5: In a twisted shaft the shear stress grows in a straight line from zero at the center to its largest value at the outer skin. The inside surface of a hollow shaft is closer to the center, so its stress is smaller: 1.0/1.5 of the outer value. Use the hollow polar moment of inertia and the inside radius.
B.hint: Shear stress is Tr/J, where r is the radius to the point you care about.

steps.text: Polar moment of inertia of the hollow section.
Radius to the inside surface.
Shear stress at that radius.
For comparison, the outer surface carries 30(1.5)/6.38 = 7.05 ksi.

traps: Using the outer radius out of habit when the question asks about the inside surface.
Putting a diameter where the formula wants a radius.
Using the solid-shaft J when the shaft is hollow.

B.topic: Stresses (axial, torsion, bending, transverse shear, thermal, thin-walled vessels)
B.statement: A steel bracket is welded from two plates into an inverted tee (a 6 in. by 1 in. flange at the bottom and a 1 in. by 8 in. stem on top, total depth 9 in.) and cantilevers 4 ft from a wall. It carries a 5-kip load at its free end, as shown. Neglect the bracket weight. The maximum tensile bending stress in the bracket (ksi) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Uses the distance from the neutral axis to the bottom of the flange (3.07 in.). That gives the compressive stress at the bottom, not the tension at the top.
Uses c = 9/2 = 4.5 in. as if the section were symmetric.
Correct: the neutral axis is 3.07 in. above the bottom, I = 112.6 in.^4, and the top of the stem (5.93 in. above the neutral axis) is in tension: 240(5.93)/112.6 = 12.6 ksi.
Adds the two plates' own moments of inertia but forgets the parallel-axis terms, so I is far too small.
B.eli5: A cantilever with a load at its tip bends downward, which stretches the top of the beam and squeezes the bottom. The biggest moment is at the wall: 5 kips times 4 ft. For an unsymmetric shape, first find the neutral axis (it sits low, near the heavy flange), then the moment of inertia about it. The top of the stem is far from the neutral axis and on the stretched side, so that is where tension is largest.
B.hint: A cantilever puts the top fibers in tension. Locate the centroid of the tee before using Mc/I.

steps.text: Maximum moment at the wall.
Centroid measured up from the bottom of the flange.
Moment of inertia about the centroid (parallel-axis theorem).
The tension side is the top of the stem, at the distance from the neutral axis below.
Maximum tensile stress.

traps: Using half the depth for c on an unsymmetric section.
Using the distance to the wrong face: under negative moment the top is in tension.
Forgetting the A d^2 terms when building I.
Leaving the span in feet while the section is in inches.

B.topic: Deformations (axial, torsional twist, beam deflection, thermal)
B.statement: A simply supported rectangular timber formwork beam (strongback) is replaced by one of the same species, the same width and the same span, but twice the depth. The concrete load on it is unchanged; neglect self-weight. The midspan deflection of the new beam, as a fraction of the old one, is:
choiceNotes: Correct: deflection is inversely proportional to I = bh^3/12, and doubling h multiplies I by 8.
Treats the stiffness as growing with h^2, which is how the section modulus (and so the bending stress) changes, not the deflection.
Treats the stiffness as growing in direct proportion to depth.
Assumes deflection depends only on the load and span, so it does not change.
B.eli5: How much a beam sags depends on its moment of inertia, and for a rectangle that grows with the depth cubed. Twice as deep means 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 times stiffer, so it sags one eighth as much. Depth is the cheapest way to make a beam stiffer.
B.hint: Deflection is proportional to 1/(EI), and I for a rectangle is bh^3/12.

steps.text: Midspan deflection of a simply supported beam under uniform load.
Only I changes; for a rectangle I grows with the cube of depth.
Deflection ratio.

traps: Mixing up how stress changes with depth (1/h^2) and how deflection changes (1/h^3).
Assuming that doubling a dimension simply halves the deflection.

B.topic: Deformations (axial, torsional twist, beam deflection, thermal)
B.statement: A short square reinforced concrete pier, 16 in. by 16 in., is 12 ft tall and reinforced with eight #9 bars (total steel area $8.00\ \text{in}^2$), with the cross section shown. Take $E_c = 3{,}600$ ksi and $E_s = 29{,}000$ ksi. Both materials stay elastic and are perfectly bonded. Under an axial load of 500 kips, the shortening of the pier (in.) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Leaves the height in feet (12 instead of 144 in.).
Treats the whole 256-square-inch section as steel.
Correct: the concrete and steel shorten together, so the axial stiffness is E_c A_c + E_s A_s = 1,124,800 kips, and 500(144)/1,124,800 = 0.0640 in.
Ignores the bars and uses the gross concrete area alone.
B.eli5: The concrete and the steel bars are glued together, so they squeeze by the same amount. Together they act like two springs side by side: their stiffnesses add. Steel is about eight times stiffer than concrete, so the bars help more than their small area suggests. Add E times A for each material, then use the usual PL over AE.
B.hint: Equal shortening means the axial stiffnesses add: use E_c A_c + E_s A_s in place of AE.

steps.text: Net concrete area (gross area minus the bars).
Combined axial stiffness of the two materials in parallel.
Height in inches.
Shortening.

traps: Ignoring the reinforcement: the bars carry a real share of the load.
Leaving the length in feet while the stiffness is in kips and inches.
Counting the bar area twice by not subtracting it from the gross concrete area (a small error here, but a habit to avoid).

B.topic: Deformations (axial, torsional twist, beam deflection, thermal)
B.statement: A steel balcony beam ($E = 29{,}000$ ksi, $I = 110\ \text{in}^4$) cantilevers 8 ft from a building wall. It carries a uniform load of 0.5 kip/ft over its full length and a 2-kip railing load at its free end, as shown. The deflection at the free end (in.) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Counts only the uniform load and forgets the railing load.
Counts only the railing load and forgets the uniform load.
Uses the simply supported formula 5wL^4/384EI for the uniform load instead of the cantilever formula wL^4/8EI.
Correct: superpose the two cantilever cases, 0.139 in. from the uniform load plus 0.185 in. from the tip load = 0.324 in.
B.eli5: When two loads act on the same elastic beam, the sag from each can be found on its own and then added. The handbook gives the tip deflection of a cantilever for a uniform load (wL^4/8EI) and for a tip load (PL^3/3EI). Put everything in kips and inches first: 0.5 kip/ft is 0.0417 kip/in., and 8 ft is 96 in.
B.hint: Superposition: add the cantilever tip deflection for the uniform load to the one for the end load, all in kip and inch units.

steps.text: Convert to kip and inch units.
Tip deflection from the uniform load.
Tip deflection from the end load.
Superpose.

traps: Leaving w in kip/ft while L is in inches, which inflates the uniform-load part twelvefold.
Taking a formula from the simply supported table instead of the cantilever table.
Answering with only one of the two loads.

B.topic: Deformations (axial, torsional twist, beam deflection, thermal)
B.statement: The extension stem of a buried water valve is a solid steel rod ($G = 11{,}500$ ksi) 1.5 in. in diameter and 6 ft long. Turning the valve requires a torque of 8 kip-in. at the bottom of the stem. The angle of twist of the stem between the operating nut and the valve (degrees) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Gets the angle in radians (0.101) and reports it as degrees.
Leaves the length in feet (6 instead of 72 in.).
Uses the modulus of elasticity E = 29,000 ksi instead of the shear modulus G.
Correct: J = 0.497 in.^4, the twist is 8(72)/(11,500 x 0.497) = 0.101 rad, which is 5.77 degrees.
B.eli5: A long thin rod twists like a spring when you turn one end. The twist is torque times length divided by G times J. With the length in inches, the formula gives radians; multiply by 180/pi to get degrees. Here the stem twists almost 6 degrees before the valve starts to turn.
B.hint: phi = TL/(GJ) gives radians. Use G (not E), inches, and convert at the end.

steps.text: Polar moment of inertia of the solid rod.
Length in inches.
Angle of twist in radians.
Convert to degrees.

traps: Using E where the formula needs the shear modulus G.
Forgetting that TL/GJ is in radians.
Using I = pi d^4/64 instead of J = pi d^4/32.

B.topic: Combined stresses, principal stresses, Mohr's circle
B.statement: The plane stress element shown is taken from a gusset plate of a steel truss. The algebraically smallest (most compressive) principal stress in the plane of the element (MPa) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Correct: the Mohr circle center is 30 MPa and its radius is 75 MPa, so the smaller principal stress is 30 - 75 = -45 MPa.
Reads the y-face stress as if it were already principal, ignoring the shear.
Uses (sigma_x - sigma_y)/2 = 60 as the center instead of (sigma_x + sigma_y)/2 = 30.
This is the larger principal stress, 30 + 75 = 105 MPa.
B.eli5: The figure shows 90 MPa pulling on the x faces, 30 MPa pushing on the y faces, and 45 MPa of shear. Mohr's circle turns that into the extreme normal stresses. Its center is the average normal stress, (90 - 30)/2 = 30 MPa, and its radius is the hypotenuse of 60 and 45, which is 75 MPa. The two principal stresses are center plus and minus radius: 105 and -45 MPa.
B.hint: Center C = (sigma_x + sigma_y)/2, radius R from half the difference and the shear; the smaller principal stress is C - R.

steps.text: Read the element: tension on the x faces, compression on the y faces.
Center of Mohr's circle.
Radius.
Smaller principal stress.

traps: Dropping the minus sign on the compressive stress when computing the center.
Swapping the sum and difference of the normal stresses between the center and the radius.
Reporting the larger principal stress when the question asks for the smaller one.

B.topic: Combined stresses, principal stresses, Mohr's circle
B.statement: At one section of a simply supported glulam beam with the solid 6 in. by 12 in. rectangular section shown, the internal shear is 9 kips and the internal bending moment is 7.5 kip-ft (positive, sagging). Point a is 3 in. below the neutral axis. The maximum principal stress at point a (psi) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Gives only the bending stress at a and ignores the shear stress.
Correct: the bending stress is 312.5 psi (tension) and the shear stress is 140.6 psi, so the larger principal stress is 156.3 + 210.2 = 366 psi.
Uses Q for the whole half section (108 in.^3), which is the shear at the neutral axis, not at point a.
Uses the full bending stress instead of half of it inside the square root.
B.eli5: Point a feels two things at once: a pull along the beam from bending, and a sliding shear from the vertical shear force. The bending part is My/I. The shear part is VQ/(Ib), where Q is for the area below point a only. Mohr's circle combines them: half the normal stress, plus the radius made from half the normal stress and the shear.
B.hint: Find sigma = My/I and tau = VQ/(Ib) at point a, then sigma_1 = sigma/2 + sqrt((sigma/2)^2 + tau^2).

steps.text: Section properties.
Bending stress at a (tension, below the neutral axis under positive moment). M = 90 kip-in.
First moment of the area below point a (6 in. by 3 in., centroid 4.5 in. from the neutral axis).
Transverse shear stress at a.
Maximum principal stress (sigma_y = 0).

traps: Using Q for the full half section: that gives the shear stress at the neutral axis, not at point a.
Forgetting to halve the normal stress inside the Mohr radius.
Leaving the moment in kip-ft while the section is in inches.

B.topic: Combined stresses, principal stresses, Mohr's circle
B.statement: A solid circular shaft carries only a torque, and the shear stress at its outer surface is 9 ksi. The maximum tensile normal stress at the outer surface, and the planes on which it acts, are:

choices.text: 0 ksi, since a shaft in pure torsion has no normal stress
4.5 ksi, on planes at 45° to the shaft axis
9 ksi, on planes perpendicular to the shaft axis
9 ksi, on planes at 45° to the shaft axis

choiceNotes: True only for planes perpendicular and parallel to the axis. On inclined planes, pure shear produces normal stress.
Halves the shear stress as if the Mohr radius were tau/2. For pure shear the radius is tau itself.
Right size, wrong planes: on the cross-section (perpendicular to the axis) the stress is pure shear, with no normal stress.
Correct: pure shear gives a Mohr circle centered at the origin with radius 9 ksi, so the principal stresses are +9 and -9 ksi, on planes at 45° to the axis.
B.eli5: Twist a piece of chalk and it snaps along a spiral at 45°. That is because pure shear is the same as equal tension and compression on planes turned 45°. The tension there is as big as the shear, 9 ksi. Brittle materials fail in tension, so they break on that 45° helix.
B.hint: Draw Mohr's circle for pure shear: center at zero, radius equal to tau.

steps.text: On the shaft surface the element is in pure shear.
Mohr's circle center and radius.
Principal stresses.
On Mohr's circle the principal points are 90° from the shear points, so on the element they are 45° from the shaft axis.

traps: Thinking that no normal stress on the cross-section means no normal stress anywhere.
Forgetting that angles on Mohr's circle are double the angles on the element.

A.topic: Mix design of concrete and asphalt
A.statement: A ready-mix plant batches the culvert headwall mix in the table on a saturated-surface-dry (SSD) basis. On the day of the pour the coarse aggregate stockpile is wet, but the fine aggregate stockpile is drier than SSD. The weight of water (lb) to add at the mixer per cubic yard is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Subtracts the full stockpile moisture of both aggregates (2.4% and 0.5%) as free water, ignoring that part of it is absorbed and that the sand is below its absorption.
Treats the dry sand like the wet gravel and subtracts its 12 lb as well, when the sand actually takes 12 lb out of the mix water.
Correct: the coarse aggregate brings about 28 lb of free water (subtract) and the dry sand soaks up about 12 lb (add back): 285 - 28 + 12 = 269 lb.
Adds the coarse aggregate's free water instead of subtracting it, and subtracts the sand's deficit instead of adding it: the signs are reversed.
A.eli5: The recipe assumes every stone is exactly "damp inside, dry on the surface". Today the gravel is dripping, so it carries extra water into the mixer and you pour less from the hose. The sand is thirsty, so it will drink some of the hose water and you must pour a little more to make up for it.
A.hint: For each aggregate the free water is its oven-dry weight times (moisture minus absorption). A negative value means the aggregate takes water from the mix.

steps.text: Oven-dry weight of each aggregate from its SSD weight.
Free water carried by the coarse aggregate (moisture above absorption).
Free water of the fine aggregate. It is below its absorption, so the value is negative: the sand absorbs water from the mix.
Water to add at the mixer is the SSD design water minus the free water brought in by the aggregates.

traps: Using the total moisture content instead of moisture minus absorption: only the water above SSD is free to join the mix.
Assuming every aggregate correction is subtracted. An aggregate drier than SSD needs extra water, so its correction is added.
Mixing up the bases: absorption and moisture are percentages of the oven-dry weight, not of the SSD weight.

A.topic: Mix design of concrete and asphalt
A.statement: A sidewalk mix is proportioned by the absolute volume method for 1 yd$^3$. Per cubic yard it has 564 lb of cement (specific gravity 3.15), 282 lb of water, 1,850 lb of SSD coarse aggregate (bulk SSD specific gravity 2.68) and 6% entrained air. The fine aggregate has a bulk SSD specific gravity of 2.62. The SSD weight of fine aggregate (lb) needed to complete the cubic yard is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Takes the 6% air as 6 ft$^3$ instead of 6% of 27 ft$^3$ (1.62 ft$^3$), which leaves far too little room for sand.
Correct: the other ingredients fill 20.07 ft$^3$, the sand fills the remaining 6.93 ft$^3$, which weighs 6.93 x 2.62 x 62.4 = 1,133 lb.
Finds the right sand volume but converts it to weight with the coarse aggregate's specific gravity (2.68) instead of the sand's (2.62).
Forgets the entrained air, so the sand is given the 1.62 ft$^3$ that the air bubbles occupy.
A.eli5: A cubic yard is a 27 cubic foot box. Pour in the cement, the water, the gravel and the air bubbles, and measure how much room each one takes. Whatever room is left is for the sand. Then turn that space back into pounds using how heavy the sand is.
A.hint: Absolute volume of each ingredient is its weight divided by (specific gravity x 62.4 lb/ft$^3$). Air is a percent of the 27 ft$^3$.

steps.text: Absolute volume of cement, water and coarse aggregate.
Volume of entrained air.
The fine aggregate fills what is left of the cubic yard.
Convert the volume to SSD weight with the sand's own specific gravity.

traps: Leaving out the air: on an air-entrained mix it is a real share of the yard.
Using the wrong specific gravity when converting the sand volume back to weight.
Forgetting the 62.4 lb/ft$^3$ unit weight of water when dividing by specific gravity.

A.topic: Mix design of concrete and asphalt
A.statement: A Superpave trial specimen for a county road overlay has bulk specific gravity $G_{mb} = 2.352$ and maximum specific gravity $G_{mm} = 2.461$. The binder content is 5.2% by total weight of mix, and the aggregate bulk specific gravity is $G_{sb} = 2.665$. The voids filled with asphalt, VFA (%), is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Stops at VMA minus air voids (16.3 - 4.4 = 11.9%), which is the volume of effective binder, not the share of the VMA it fills.
Inverts the ratio: air voids divided by VMA is the share of the VMA that is still empty.
Computes VMA without the aggregate fraction $P_s$, getting 11.7% instead of 16.3%.
A.eli5: Picture the gaps between the stones in the compacted mix (VMA). Some of that gap space is filled with asphalt and the rest is air. VFA asks: of all the gap space, what share is asphalt? Find the total gaps, take away the air, and divide by the total gaps.
A.hint: Find the air voids from $G_{mb}$ and $G_{mm}$, the VMA from $G_{mb}$, $P_s$ and $G_{sb}$, then VFA = (VMA - $V_a$)/VMA.

steps.text: Air voids.
Aggregate share of the mix is $P_s = 100 - 5.2 = 94.8\%$. Voids in the mineral aggregate:
Voids filled with asphalt.

A.handbookFormula: V_a = 100(1 - G_{mb}/G_{mm}),\ VMA = 100 - G_{mb}P_s/G_{sb},\ VFA = 100(VMA - V_a)/VMA
traps: Leaving $P_s$ out of the VMA formula: VMA is based on the aggregate share of the mix, not the whole mix.
Confusing VMA, VFA and air voids: VFA is a share of VMA, not of the total volume.
Using the binder content (5.2) where the aggregate content (94.8) belongs.

A.statement: A quarry wants to sell crushed limestone as base course for a haul road. The specification limits how much the coarse aggregate may break down and wear when tumbled with steel spheres in a rotating drum. The test that measures this is the:
choiceNotes: Correct: the Los Angeles test tumbles the aggregate with steel spheres and reports the percent of mass lost through a No. 12 sieve as a measure of toughness and abrasion resistance.
Marshall stability is a load test on a compacted asphalt specimen, not on loose aggregate.
The sand equivalent test measures the clay and fine dust in fine aggregate, not resistance to wear.
Charpy measures the impact energy of a notched metal bar, mainly to find the ductile-to-brittle transition of steel.
A.eli5: Put the stones in a big drum with steel balls and spin it. Weak stones chip and turn to dust, strong ones stay whole. Weigh the dust: less dust means tougher rock.
A.hint: Which test uses a rotating drum and steel spheres?

steps.text: Resistance of coarse aggregate to impact and abrasion is measured by tumbling a graded sample with steel spheres in a rotating drum for a set number of revolutions.
The result is the percent loss: the mass that passes the No. 12 sieve afterwards divided by the original mass. That is the Los Angeles abrasion test.

traps: Picking a test that sounds like toughness but applies to a different material (Charpy for metals, Marshall for compacted asphalt).

A.statement: An engineer uses a rebound (Schmidt) hammer on the slabs of an older parking garage. Which statement about the readings is most appropriate?

choices.text: They indicate surface hardness and need a core correlation to estimate strength.
They give the in-place compressive strength directly, so no cores need drilling.
They locate the reinforcing bars and measure the depth of concrete cover.
They detect voids and cracks deep inside the slab from the time of travel of a pulse.

choiceNotes: Correct: the rebound number depends on the hardness of the top inch or so of concrete; it is good for finding weak or uneven areas, and it estimates strength only through a correlation with cores from the same concrete.
The rebound number is affected by surface carbonation, moisture, finish and aggregate, so it cannot replace cores for strength.
That is a cover meter (an electromagnetic device), not a rebound hammer.
That is ultrasonic pulse velocity, which times a sound wave through the member.
A.eli5: The hammer bounces a spring-loaded plunger off the slab and measures how far it bounces back. A hard surface gives a big bounce. It only feels the skin of the slab, so it is great for saying "this area is softer than that one", but to turn bounces into psi you need to crush a few drilled cores and compare.
A.hint: The hammer only touches the surface.

steps.text: The rebound hammer measures the rebound of a spring-driven mass off the surface, which depends on the hardness of the near-surface concrete.
Surface conditions (carbonation, moisture, finish) change the reading, so the hammer is used to compare uniformity; strength estimates need a correlation with cores from the same structure.

A.handbookFormula: \text{Rebound number} \to \text{surface hardness (correlate with cores for } f'_c)
traps: Reading the hammer's strength chart as the in-place strength of the slab.
Mixing up the nondestructive tests: rebound hammer (surface hardness), cover meter (rebar), pulse velocity (internal flaws).

A.statement: The figure shows the first part of the engineering stress-strain curve from a tension test on an aluminum alloy used for a pedestrian bridge railing. The yield strength (ksi) by the 0.2% offset method is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Reads the curve at a total strain of 0.002 instead of drawing a line parallel to the elastic part from a strain of 0.002.
The stress where the curve first bends away from a straight line: that is the proportional limit, which is lower than the offset yield strength.
Correct: the elastic slope is 10,000 ksi; a line of that slope through a strain of 0.002 meets the curve at a strain of 0.006 and 40 ksi.
Takes the highest stress shown on the chart, which is past yield and heading toward the tensile strength.
A.eli5: Metals do not have a sharp "now it bends for good" point, so engineers agree on a rule. Slide a copy of the straight starting line 0.002 to the right, and where it hits the curve is the yield strength. It is the stress that leaves the bar 0.2% longer after you let go.
A.hint: Find the slope of the straight part, then draw a line with that slope starting at a strain of 0.002 on the axis.

steps.text: Elastic slope from the straight part of the curve: 20 ksi at a strain of 0.002.
Offset line: same slope, starting at a strain of 0.002.
The offset line passes through 20 ksi at 0.004, 30 ksi at 0.005 and 40 ksi at 0.006. The curve also passes through 40 ksi at a strain of 0.006, so they meet there.

A.handbookFormula: \sigma = E\varepsilon;\ \text{yield strength by the 0.2\% offset method}
traps: Reading the stress at a total strain of 0.002 instead of drawing the offset line.
Calling the proportional limit the yield strength.
Drawing the offset line from the origin, or with a slope that does not match the elastic part.

A.statement: A precast concrete girder carries the same permanent dead load for years. Its strain keeps growing slowly with time even though the load, temperature and humidity around it do not change. This time-dependent deformation under sustained load is called:
choiceNotes: Fatigue is damage from repeated (cyclic) loading, not from a load that stays constant.
Drying shrinkage comes from moisture loss and happens with or without load; here the humidity does not change and the strain is caused by the load.
Correct: creep is deformation that keeps increasing with time under a constant sustained stress.
Relaxation is the opposite case: the strain is held constant and the stress drops with time (for example in a prestressing strand).
A.eli5: Lean on a sponge with the same weight all day and it slowly squashes further, even though you are not pushing harder. Concrete does the same thing, very slowly, under its own permanent load. That slow squish is creep.
A.hint: Constant load, growing strain.

steps.text: The load is constant and the environment is unchanged, so neither cyclic loading nor moisture loss explains the growth.
Strain that increases with time at constant stress is creep (the Handbook lists it as time-dependent deformation under load).

traps: Confusing creep (constant stress, strain grows) with relaxation (constant strain, stress drops).
Blaming shrinkage, which needs drying and does not need a load.
