A.topic: Mix design of concrete and asphalt
A.statement: A bridge abutment will be exposed to freezing and thawing with deicing salts, so its concrete must be air-entrained and reach an average 28-day strength of 4,500 psi. The supplier's trial-batch curves are shown. The mix needs 270 lb of water per cubic yard, and fly ash will make up 15% of the total cementitious materials by weight. The portland cement content (lb/yd$^3$) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Reads the non-air-entrained curve (w/cm = 0.55), which overstates the strength this air-entrained mix will reach at a given ratio.
Correct: the air-entrained curve gives w/cm = 0.45, so cementitious = 270/0.45 = 600 lb, of which 85% is cement: 510 lb.
Stops at the total cementitious materials and forgets that 15% of it is fly ash.
Adds 15% to the cementitious content instead of taking 15% of it as fly ash.
A.eli5: Air bubbles protect concrete from freezing but make it a little weaker, so it has to use the air-entrained curve, which needs less water per pound of cement. Read the ratio at 4,500 psi, work out how much "glue" (cement plus fly ash) goes with 270 lb of water, then keep the 85% that is cement.
A.hint: Use the curve that matches the exposure, then w/cm = water / (cement + fly ash).

steps.text: Freeze-thaw exposure needs air entrainment, so read the air-entrained curve at 4,500 psi.
Total cementitious materials from the water content.
Fly ash is 15% of the cementitious materials, so portland cement is 85%.

traps: Reading the non-air-entrained curve for an air-entrained mix.
Stopping at total cementitious materials when the question asks for cement only.
Computing fly ash as 15% of the cement instead of 15% of the total cementitious materials.

A.statement: The hot-mix asphalt surface at a truck weigh station is rutting badly under slow, heavy wheel loads in summer. For the replacement mix, which change is most likely to improve rutting resistance?

choices.text: Raise the binder content above the optimum to make the mix more flexible.
Use a binder with a lower high-temperature performance grade.
Allow more flat and elongated particles in the coarse aggregate.
Replace the rounded river gravel with crushed, angular stone.

choiceNotes: Extra binder fills the voids, lubricates the stone skeleton and causes bleeding and more rutting.
A lower high-temperature grade is a softer binder at summer temperatures, which ruts more, not less.
Flat and elongated particles break during compaction and under traffic and do not lock together well.
Correct: crushed, angular faces interlock and give the stone skeleton internal friction, which is what resists permanent deformation.
A.eli5: Rutting is the mix slowly sliding out from under heavy tires on a hot day. Round pebbles roll past each other like marbles; broken stone with sharp faces locks together like a pile of bricks. Locked-together stone does not get pushed aside.
A.hint: Rutting resistance comes mostly from the stone skeleton, not the binder.

steps.text: Rutting is permanent deformation from shear flow of the mix at high temperature under slow, heavy loads.
Shear resistance comes from aggregate interlock (internal friction), which angular crushed faces provide; more or softer binder and weak flat particles all reduce it.

A.handbookFormula: \text{Rut resistance} \uparrow \text{ with aggregate angularity and stiffer binder}
traps: Thinking more binder makes a stronger mix: above optimum it makes the mix unstable.
Reading "lower grade" as stronger: the high-temperature grade must go up for hot, slow traffic.

A.statement: A 500 g sample of concrete sand for a bridge deck is sieved, and the table lists the mass caught on each sieve and in the pan. The fineness modulus of the sand is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Adds the individual percents retained instead of the cumulative percents.
Correct: cumulative percents retained are 0, 3, 15, 32, 54, 78 and 94; their sum is 276, and 276/100 = 2.76.
Sums the cumulative percents passing on the No. 4 through No. 100 sieves (97 + 85 + 68 + 46 + 22 + 6 = 324) instead of the cumulative percents retained.
Includes the pan (100%) in the sum; the pan is not one of the standard sieves.
A.eli5: Count how much sand gets stopped by each sieve, adding up as you go from coarse to fine. Add those running totals as percents and divide by 100. A bigger number means a coarser sand.
A.hint: Turn the masses into cumulative percent retained on each sieve from 3/8 in. down to No. 100, leave out the pan, add and divide by 100.

steps.text: Cumulative mass retained, from coarse to fine: 0, 15, 75, 160, 270, 390 and 470 g. As a percent of 500 g:
Fineness modulus: sum of cumulative percents retained on the standard sieves (pan excluded), divided by 100.

traps: Using the percent retained on each sieve instead of the running (cumulative) total.
Counting the pan as a sieve.
Working with percent passing instead of percent retained.

B.topic: Mix design of concrete and asphalt
B.statement: A trial batch for a parking structure slab was proportioned to make exactly 1 yd$^3$ with these batch weights: cement 600 lb, water 300 lb, coarse aggregate 1,850 lb and fine aggregate 1,270 lb. The fresh concrete is tested and its unit weight is 146.0 lb/ft$^3$. The cement content (lb/yd$^3$) actually delivered in the concrete is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Correct: the batch weighs 4,020 lb and yields 4,020 / 146.0 = 27.53 ft$^3$, more than 27 ft$^3$, so the 600 lb of cement is spread over a little more than 1 yd$^3$: 600 x 27 / 27.53 = 588 lb/yd$^3$.
Assumes the batch made exactly 1 yd$^3$ as designed. The unit weight test shows it did not.
Multiplies by the relative yield (1.020) instead of dividing: more volume means less cement per cubic yard, not more.
Leaves the 300 lb of water out of the batch weight, so the yield comes out as only 25.5 ft$^3$. Water is part of the concrete and counts.
B.eli5: You followed a recipe meant to fill one bucket, but the mix filled a bucket and a little more. The same cement is now spread through more concrete, so each bucket gets slightly less cement than the recipe says.
B.hint: Yield is the total batch weight divided by the measured unit weight. Compare it with 27 ft$^3$.

steps.text: Total weight of everything in the batch, water included.
Yield is the volume that weight actually occupies.
Relative yield: the batch made about 2% more concrete than designed.
Cement actually in each cubic yard.

traps: Leaving water out of the total batch weight. Every ingredient that goes into the drum ends up in the concrete.
Multiplying by the relative yield instead of dividing. Over-yield dilutes the cement.
Mixing ft$^3$ and yd$^3$: the yield comes out in ft$^3$, and 1 yd$^3$ = 27 ft$^3$.

B.topic: Mix design of concrete and asphalt
B.statement: A compacted asphalt specimen for an airport taxiway mix weighs 1,215.6 g dry in air, 1,219.0 g saturated-surface-dry in air and 704.3 g submerged in water. The mix has 5.5% binder by total weight of mix, a maximum specific gravity $G_{mm} = 2.468$, and the aggregate bulk specific gravity is $G_{sb} = 2.680$. The voids in the mineral aggregate, VMA (%), are most nearly:
choiceNotes: This is the air void content, $100(G_{mm} - G_{mb})/G_{mm}$, not the VMA. VMA also includes the voids that the binder fills.
Leaves out the aggregate fraction $P_s = 94.5\%$ and uses $100\,G_{mb}/G_{sb}$ as if the whole specimen were aggregate.
Uses the dry mass minus the submerged mass (1,215.6 - 704.3) as the volume. The specimen volume comes from the SSD mass minus the submerged mass.
B.eli5: Picture the specimen as a box of stones. VMA is the share of the box that is not stone: the binder plus the air. First you find how heavy the box is for its size, then you work out how much of that size the stones themselves take up.
B.hint: Find $G_{mb}$ from the three weighings first. In the VMA formula the aggregate is $P_s = 100 - P_b$ percent of the mix.

steps.text: Bulk specific gravity of the compacted specimen: dry mass over its volume, which is the SSD mass minus the submerged mass.
Aggregate share of the mix by weight.
Volume of aggregate as a percent of the specimen, then VMA is the rest.

traps: Using the dry mass instead of the SSD mass to find the specimen volume.
Forgetting the $P_s$ term: the specimen is not all aggregate.
Answering with air voids. Air voids, VMA and VFA are three different ratios; VMA = air voids + effective binder volume.

B.topic: Mix design of concrete and asphalt
B.statement: At a drum plant producing hot-mix asphalt for a rural highway, the binder pump is set to add 6.0 lb of asphalt binder for every 100 lb of dry aggregate. The binder content (%) by total weight of mix, as a mix design reports it, is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Correct: every 106 lb of mix holds 6.0 lb of binder, so $P_b = 6.0/106 = 5.7\%$.
This is the binder content by weight of aggregate, the number the pump was set to. The mix design basis is total weight of mix.
Converts in the wrong direction, $6.0/(100 - 6.0)$, as if 6.0% were already by weight of mix and had to be put on an aggregate basis.
This is the aggregate share of the mix, $100/106$, not the binder share.
B.eli5: For every 100 pounds of stones you pour in 6 pounds of binder, so the finished mix weighs 106 pounds. The binder is 6 out of those 106, a little under 6 percent.
B.hint: The total weight of mix is aggregate plus binder.

steps.text: Weight of mix made from 100 lb of aggregate.
Binder as a percent of the total mix.

traps: Reporting the plant setting (by weight of aggregate) as the binder content (by weight of mix).
Dividing by 94 instead of 106: that converts the other way.

B.statement: During acceptance testing of concrete for a bridge approach slab, the technician fills and rods the slump cone, lifts it, and the concrete settles as shown: one side breaks away and slides down along an inclined plane. This is the first test on this truck. Under the standard slump test method, the most appropriate action is to:

choices.text: record the slump measured from the top of the cone height down to the lowest point of the broken-off piece
reject the truck, because a sheared sample proves the concrete is out of specification
add water to the truck to make the mix more plastic, remix, and repeat the test
disregard this result and make a new test on another portion of the same sample

choiceNotes: A sheared specimen gives no valid slump at all. Measuring to the lowest point of the slid piece would also be the wrong spot even for a valid test (slump is measured at the displaced original center of the top).

One shear can come from the sampling or rodding, not the concrete. Only if two consecutive tests shear does the method say the concrete probably lacks the plasticity and cohesion for the test to apply.
Adding water raises the water-cement ratio and lowers strength and durability. A test result is never fixed by changing the concrete to suit the test.
Correct: the slump test method says to disregard a test where a portion shears off and to repeat it on another portion of the sample.
B.eli5: If the sand castle falls over sideways, you cannot measure how much it sagged. You throw that try away and build another one from the same bucket. If it falls sideways again, then the sand itself is the problem.
B.hint: Ask whether a lopsided specimen can give any meaningful slump at all, and what the method says about one bad test versus two.

steps.text: Slump measures how far the top of an intact, roughly symmetric cone of concrete settles. When one side shears off and slides, the shape no longer reflects consistency, so there is no valid slump to record.
The test method (ASTM C143) handles this directly: disregard the test and make a new one on another portion of the sample.
Only if two consecutive tests shear is the concrete judged to lack the plasticity and cohesion the slump test needs. Rejecting the load or adding water on the first shear is not supported.

B.handbookFormula: Slump = drop of the displaced original center of the top surface (valid only if the specimen does not shear)
traps: Recording a number from a sheared specimen.
Adding water at the site to fix a test result.
Rejecting a load on one test that may reflect poor technique.

B.statement: The figure shows the sieve analysis of a crushed aggregate blend proposed for an asphalt base course on a county road. Using the Superpave definition, the nominal maximum aggregate size of the blend is:
choiceNotes: This is the first sieve that retains more than 10% (only 84% passes it). The nominal maximum size is one sieve size larger than that sieve.
Correct: 97% passes the 3/4 in. sieve and 84% passes the 1/2 in. sieve, so the 1/2 in. sieve is the first to retain more than 10%, and the NMAS is one size larger, 3/4 in.
This is the Superpave maximum aggregate size, one sieve larger than the nominal maximum size (and the smallest sieve that passes 100%).
This is the largest sieve in the analysis. It tells you nothing about the size of the aggregate, only where the stack started.
B.eli5: A few stones caught on the 3/4 inch screen do not count, but once a sizable share (more than a tenth) gets caught on the 1/2 inch screen, the aggregate is said to be "nominally" one screen size bigger than that: 3/4 inch.
B.hint: Find the first sieve, from the top, where less than 90% passes. The nominal maximum size is one sieve larger.

steps.text: Read percent passing from the top of the stack: 1-1/2 in. 100%, 1 in. 100%, 3/4 in. 97%, 1/2 in. 84%.
Percent retained (cumulative) is 100 minus percent passing: 3/4 in. retains 3%, 1/2 in. retains 16%. The first sieve to retain more than 10% is the 1/2 in. sieve.
Superpave nominal maximum aggregate size is one sieve size larger than that first sieve: 3/4 in. (The maximum aggregate size would be one size larger again, 1 in.)

B.handbookFormula: \text{NMAS} = \text{one sieve larger than the first sieve retaining} > 10\%
traps: Answering the first sieve that retains more than 10% instead of the sieve one size larger.
Confusing nominal maximum size with maximum size, which is one sieve larger still.
Reading percent passing as percent retained.

B.statement: A 6 in. x 12 in. concrete cylinder from a canal lining pour is tested on its side between two bearing strips, as shown, and splits at a total load of 42,000 lb. The splitting tensile strength (psi) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Correct: $T = 2P/(\pi L D) = 2(42{,}000)/(\pi \times 12 \times 6) = 371$ psi.
Divides the load by the projected area $L D$ only. The splitting formula has the factor $2/\pi$ from elastic theory.
Uses the radius (3 in.) instead of the diameter in $2P/(\pi L D)$, doubling the answer.
Treats it as a compression test, dividing the load by the circular end area $\pi D^2/4$. The load acts along the length, across the diameter.
B.eli5: Squeezing a cylinder across its middle makes it want to split open along that line, the way a log splits under a wedge. The formula turns the squeezing load into the pulling-apart stress across that split face.
B.hint: The splitting tensile strength is $T = 2P/(\pi L D)$ with the full diameter.

steps.text: The load squeezes the cylinder across one diameter along its full length. Elastic theory gives a nearly uniform tension across that diametral plane.
Substitute the failure load and dimensions.

traps: Using the radius instead of the diameter.
Dropping the factor of 2 or the $\pi$.
Using the end area as if the cylinder were crushed lengthwise.

B.statement: A highway agency is choosing a metal for guardrail anchor plates that must absorb as much energy as possible before they fracture in a crash. The figure shows the engineering stress-strain curves of four candidate metals, each to fracture (x). The most appropriate choice is:
choiceNotes: Metal A has the highest strength and stiffness but fractures at only about 4% strain, so the area under its curve is small. Strength is not toughness.
Metal B stretches the most but at low stress, so its area is smaller than C's. Ductility alone is not toughness.
Correct: energy absorbed to fracture per unit volume (toughness) is the area under the curve, and C combines high stress with large strain, giving the largest area.
Metal D has moderate strength and little elongation; its area is the second smallest.
B.eli5: The energy a metal can soak up before breaking is like strength times stretch. A very strong metal that snaps early, or a very stretchy metal that is weak, both soak up less than one that is fairly strong and stretches a long way.
B.hint: Energy absorbed per unit volume up to fracture is the area under the stress-strain curve.

steps.text: Energy absorbed per unit volume up to fracture (modulus of toughness) is the area under the whole stress-strain curve.
Estimate each area as roughly average stress times fracture strain: A about 90 ksi x 0.04 = 3.6; B about 27 ksi x 0.42 = 11; C about 68 ksi x 0.29 = 20; D about 43 ksi x 0.12 = 5 (in.-kip/in.$^3$).
C has the largest area, so it absorbs the most energy before fracture.

traps: Picking the strongest metal: high strength with little strain gives a tall but thin area.
Picking the most ductile metal: large strain at low stress gives a long but flat area.
Confusing toughness (area to fracture) with resilience (area under the elastic part only).

B.statement: The specifications for a mountain highway overlay call for a PG 70-28 asphalt binder. The two numbers in this grade mean the binder:

choices.text: can be mixed at temperatures up to 70°C and compacted at temperatures down to 28°C
meets the specified properties at pavement temperatures from a high of 70°C down to a low of -28°C
has a penetration at 25°C between 28 and 70 tenths of a millimeter
suits a climate whose highest and lowest air temperatures are 70°F and -28°F

choiceNotes: Mixing and compaction happen far hotter (about 135 to 165°C). The PG numbers describe the pavement in service, not construction temperatures.
Correct: Performance Grading names the high and low pavement design temperatures (°C) at which the binder meets the rutting and cracking criteria.
This mixes up Performance Grading with the older penetration grading system (such as 60-70 pen), which was based on a needle test at 25°C.
The grade is in degrees Celsius and refers to pavement temperatures, which in summer run well above air temperature.
B.eli5: The label is a promise about the road's own temperature: the binder will not go soft and rut until the pavement passes 70°C, and will not turn brittle and crack until it falls below minus 28°C.
B.hint: PG stands for Performance Grade. Think about what the pavement itself experiences in summer and winter.

steps.text: In a PG grade the first number is the high pavement design temperature in °C (an average 7-day maximum); above it the binder may be too soft and rut.
The second number is the low pavement design temperature in °C, written as a minus value; below it the binder may become brittle and crack.
So PG 70-28 meets the specified properties from 70°C down to -28°C in the pavement.

traps: Reading the numbers as air temperatures or as °F.
Confusing Performance Grading with penetration or viscosity grading.

B.statement: A pedestrian bridge deck uses structural lightweight concrete with a unit weight of 115 lb/ft$^3$ and a specified compressive strength of 5,000 psi. For the deflection check, the modulus of elasticity of the concrete (ksi) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Puts $f'_c$ in ksi (5) under the square root. The formula is written for $f'_c$ in psi and gives $E_c$ in psi.
Drops the 1.5 exponent on the unit weight.
Uses the shortcut $57{,}000\sqrt{f'_c}$, which only applies to normal-weight concrete of about 145 lb/ft$^3$. Lightweight concrete is less stiff.
B.eli5: Lighter concrete has lighter, softer stones in it, so it squashes a bit more under the same load. The formula takes both the weight and the strength of the concrete into account to say how springy it is.
B.hint: Use the general formula that includes the unit weight, with $w_c$ in lb/ft$^3$ and $f'_c$ in psi.

steps.text: Modulus of elasticity of concrete from unit weight and strength (ACI 318).
Unit weight term.
Substitute, with $f'_c$ in psi.

traps: Using $57{,}000\sqrt{f'_c}$ for lightweight concrete; it overstates stiffness and understates deflection.
Putting $f'_c$ in ksi in a formula built for psi.
Forgetting the 1.5 exponent on $w_c$.

B.statement: A 12 ft long steel hanger rod ($E = 29{,}000$ ksi) in a parking garage was overloaded in an accident to point P on its stress-strain curve, shown in the figure, and then the load was removed completely. The permanent elongation of the rod (in.) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: This is the elastic recovery, $(48/29{,}000)(144)$: the part that springs back, not the part that stays.
Subtracts the 0.002 offset strain used to define yield instead of the actual elastic recovery $\sigma_P/E$: $(0.0120 - 0.002)(144) = 1.44$ in.
Correct: unloading follows a line parallel to the elastic slope, so the permanent strain is $0.0120 - 48/29{,}000 = 0.01034$, and $0.01034 \times 144 = 1.49$ in.
This is the total elongation while loaded at P, $0.0120 \times 144$. Some of it is recovered when the load comes off.
B.eli5: Pull a paper clip far enough and it stays bent, but it still springs back a little when you let go. The springy part follows the same stiffness the rod had at the start. What is left after the spring-back is the permanent stretch.
B.hint: When the load is removed, the rod recovers an elastic strain of $\sigma/E$ along a line parallel to the initial slope.

steps.text: Total strain at P, read from the figure.
Unloading is elastic, parallel to the initial slope, so the recovered strain is the stress at P over E.
Permanent (plastic) strain left after unloading.
Permanent elongation over the 12 ft = 144 in. rod.

traps: Reporting the total elongation under load instead of what remains after unloading.
Subtracting 0.002 (the offset used to define yield) instead of the actual elastic strain $\sigma/E$.
Multiplying the strain by 12 ft gives 0.124, which is in feet. Convert the length to 144 in. first.

A.statement: The hydraulic oil in the operating cylinders of a navigation lock gate has a specific gravity of 0.88 and a dynamic viscosity of $\mu = 3.2 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{lbf-sec/ft}^2$. What is its kinematic viscosity? Take the density of water as $1.94\ \text{slug/ft}^3$.
choiceNotes: Divides by the specific weight, $0.88 \times 62.4 = 54.9\ \text{lbf/ft}^3$, instead of the mass density. Kinematic viscosity needs density in slug/ft³.
Divides by the density of water, 1.94 slug/ft³, and forgets to multiply by the specific gravity of the oil.
Correct: $\rho = 0.88(1.94) = 1.707\ \text{slug/ft}^3$ and $\nu = \mu/\rho = 3.2 \times 10^{-4}/1.707 = 1.87 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{ft}^2\text{/sec}$.
Multiplies $\mu$ by $\rho$ instead of dividing. The units come out as lbf-slug-sec/ft⁵, not ft²/sec.
A.eli5: Dynamic viscosity says how hard it is to shear the oil. Kinematic viscosity divides that by how much mass the oil has per cubic foot, so you need the oil's mass density: its specific gravity times the density of water, in slugs. Then divide.
A.hint: Kinematic viscosity is dynamic viscosity divided by mass density. In US units, density is in slug/ft³.

steps.text: Find the mass density of the oil from its specific gravity.
Divide the dynamic viscosity by the density. A slug is 1 lbf-sec²/ft, so the units reduce to ft²/sec.

traps: Using specific weight (lbf/ft³) or density in lbm/ft³ instead of slug/ft³.
Forgetting to multiply the water density by the specific gravity.

A.statement: A clean glass piezometer tube with a bore of 3 mm is tapped into the crown of a water main, as shown. The water in the tube stands 850 mm above the centerline of the main. For water, $\sigma = 0.0728\ \text{N/m}$, the contact angle with clean glass is 0°, and $\gamma = 9{,}810\ \text{N/m}^3$. After correcting for capillary rise, the pressure head at the centerline of the main is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Uses the radius (1.5 mm) in place of the diameter in $h = 4\sigma\cos\beta/(\gamma d)$, which doubles the capillary rise to 19.8 mm.
Correct: the capillary rise is $4(0.0728)/(9{,}810 \times 0.003) = 0.0099\ \text{m}$, and the true head is $0.850 - 0.0099 = 0.840\ \text{m}$.
Uses $2\sigma$ instead of $4\sigma$ with the diameter, which halves the capillary rise to 4.9 mm.
Adds the capillary rise instead of subtracting it. Surface tension pulls the column up, so the tube reads high, not low.
A.eli5: In a thin glass tube, water climbs the walls by itself, so the column stands a little higher than the pressure alone would push it. Work out how much extra the tube adds and take it off the reading.
A.hint: Capillary rise is $h = 4\sigma\cos\beta/(\gamma d)$, with $d$ the tube diameter. Does it make the reading too high or too low?

steps.text: Capillary rise in a 3 mm tube, with $\cos 0° = 1$.
Water wets glass, so the meniscus pulls the column up and the tube reads high. Subtract the rise.

traps: Using the tube radius where the formula has the diameter.
Adding the capillary rise. For water in glass it is a rise, so the true head is lower than the reading.

A.statement: A bridge inspection crew works from a float made of a solid timber block 10 ft long, 6 ft wide and 1.5 ft deep. The timber has a specific gravity of 0.55. Two inspectors and their gear add 600 lb, placed at the center so the float stays level in fresh water ($\gamma = 62.4\ \text{lbf/ft}^3$). The depth $d$ to which the float sinks is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Floats only the 600 lb load and forgets the weight of the timber itself.
This is the freeboard, $1.5 - 0.985$, the part above the water, not the depth submerged.
Draft of the bare float, $0.55 \times 1.5$. It leaves out the 600 lb load.
A.eli5: A floating object sinks until the water it pushes aside weighs as much as the object and everything on it. Add the timber's weight to the crew's, then find how deep a 10 by 6 ft footprint must sit to push aside that much water.
A.hint: A floating body displaces its own total weight of water. Displaced volume is plan area times depth.

steps.text: Weight of the timber.
Total weight to be carried.
Buoyant force equals total weight; the displaced volume is the plan area times the draft.
Check: $d$ is less than 1.5 ft, so the float is not swamped. About 0.5 ft of freeboard remains.

traps: Forgetting either the timber weight or the added load.
Reporting the freeboard instead of the submerged depth.

A.statement: The upstream face of a concrete gravity dam is battered: it makes an angle of 70° with the horizontal base and leans downstream as it rises, so the reservoir sits partly on top of it. The water is 9.0 m deep at the face. Using $\gamma = 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3$, the vertical component of the hydrostatic force on the upstream face, per metre of dam length, is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Correct: the water above the face is a triangle $9.0\ \text{m}$ tall and $9.0/\tan 70° = 3.28\ \text{m}$ wide, so $F_V = 9.81(\tfrac{1}{2})(9.0)(3.28) = 145\ \text{kN/m}$.
Takes the water above the face as a rectangle, $9.0 \times 3.28$, and drops the 1/2 for the triangular wedge.
This is the horizontal component, $\tfrac{1}{2}\gamma h^2 = 397\ \text{kN/m}$, not the vertical one.
This is the full resultant normal to the face, $\gamma h_c A = 9.81(4.5)(9.0/\sin 70°) = 423\ \text{kN/m}$, not its vertical component.
A.eli5: Water pushes square onto the sloping face. Because the face leans back under the water, part of that push is downward: it equals the weight of the wedge of water sitting directly above the face.
A.hint: The vertical force on a submerged surface equals the weight of the liquid directly above it, up to the free surface.

steps.text: Horizontal run of the face over the water depth.
The water above the face is a triangular wedge per metre of length.
Vertical component equals the weight of that wedge.
Check by components: the resultant is $9.81(4.5)(9.58) = 423\ \text{kN/m}$ normal to the face, and its vertical part is $423 \cos 70° = 145\ \text{kN/m}$.

traps: Giving the horizontal component or the full resultant when the vertical component is asked.
Using $h\tan 70°$ for the run instead of $h/\tan 70°$.
Treating the wedge of water as a rectangle.

A.statement: An empty precast concrete manhole with its cover in place is set in saturated ground, as shown. It is a closed cylinder 5.0 ft in outside diameter and 10 ft tall with 4-in. walls, and it weighs 8,500 lb. Groundwater stands 8.0 ft above the bottom of the base. Ignoring soil friction on the walls, the factor of safety against flotation is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Uses the 5.0 ft diameter as a radius, so the displaced area and the uplift come out four times too large.
Takes the whole 10 ft height as submerged. Only the 8.0 ft below the water table displaces water.
Correct: uplift $= 62.4(\pi/4)(5.0)^2(8.0) = 9{,}800\ \text{lb}$ and $FS = 8{,}500/9{,}800 = 0.87$. Below 1.0, so the manhole will float.
Uses the 4.33 ft inside diameter, so $FS = 8{,}500/7{,}360 = 1.15$. The water is displaced by the whole outside of the structure, walls included.
A.eli5: The ground water pushes up on the manhole with a force equal to the weight of water it shoves aside, which is its outside footprint times the depth below the water table. Compare that with what the manhole weighs. Less weight than push means it pops up.
A.hint: Buoyant force equals the weight of water displaced: outside area times the submerged height.

steps.text: Displaced volume uses the outside diameter and the submerged height only.
Buoyant (uplift) force.
Factor of safety against flotation.
Below 1.0: the empty manhole would float, so it needs an anti-flotation collar or a heavier base.

traps: Using the inside diameter or the full height.
Treating the diameter as a radius in the area.

A.statement: A rectangular flap gate on a stormwater outfall is 1.8 m high and 1.0 m wide. It hangs vertically from a hinge along its top edge. On the land side the water surface is 3.0 m above the bottom of the gate; on the sea side the tide stands 1.2 m above the bottom of the gate. Neglecting the gate's weight and hinge friction, the horizontal force $P$ at the bottom edge needed to hold the gate closed is most nearly ($\gamma = 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3$):
choiceNotes: Places both hydrostatic forces at the centroids of their wetted areas instead of at the centers of pressure, which shortens both moment arms.
Correct: moments about the hinge, $38.14 - 9.89 = 28.25\ \text{kN·m}$, divided by the 1.8 m arm give $P = 15.7\ \text{kN}$.
Ignores the tide water on the sea side, which pushes back on the lower part of the gate.
Sets $P$ equal to the net horizontal water force, $37.08 - 7.06$. The hinge carries part of that force; $P$ comes from moments about the hinge.
A.eli5: The gate swings on its top edge, so what matters is turning effect about that hinge. Land water turns it outward, the tide turns it back, and $P$ at the bottom makes up the difference. Each water force acts lower than the middle of its wetted area, at its center of pressure.
A.hint: Take moments about the hinge. Find each force and where it acts (center of pressure), then solve for $P$ with its 1.8 m arm.

steps.text: Land side: the gate top is $3.0 - 1.8 = 1.2\ \text{m}$ deep, so its centroid is 2.1 m deep.
Center of pressure below the land surface, then its arm from the hinge (1.2 m deep).
Land-side moment about the hinge.
Sea side: the tide wets only the bottom 1.2 m, a triangular load acting 0.4 m above the bottom, which is $1.8 - 0.4 = 1.4\ \text{m}$ below the hinge.
Moments about the hinge: $P$ acts 1.8 m below it.

traps: Applying a hydrostatic force at the centroid instead of the center of pressure.
Leaving out the opposing water on the sea side.
Summing forces instead of moments: the hinge reaction is unknown, so take moments about the hinge.

A.statement: A pitot-static tube is held on the centerline of a 48-in. culvert flowing full of water. Its two leads go to a U-tube manometer filled with a gauge fluid of specific gravity 1.60, with water above the gauge fluid in both legs. The manometer reading is 9 in. The water velocity at the tube is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Correct: $\Delta p/\gamma_w = (1.60 - 1)(0.75) = 0.45\ \text{ft}$ of water, and $v = \sqrt{2(32.2)(0.45)} = 5.4\ \text{ft/sec}$.
Uses the full gauge fluid weight, $1.60 \times 0.75$, and ignores the water standing over the gauge fluid in the legs.
Adds the water column instead of subtracting it, using $(1.60 + 1)$.
Leaves the reading in inches: $h = 0.60 \times 9 = 5.4$ treated as feet.
A.eli5: The nose of the tube feels the water slamming into it; the side holes feel only the ordinary pressure. The manometer shows the difference. Because water sits on top of the gauge fluid in both legs, only the extra weight of the gauge fluid over water counts.
A.hint: For a manometer with water above the gauge fluid, $\Delta p = (\gamma_{gauge} - \gamma_w)h$. Then $v = \sqrt{2g\,\Delta p/\gamma_w}$.

steps.text: Convert the reading to feet.
Pressure difference as a head of the flowing water, using the difference in specific weights.
Pitot tube velocity.

traps: Ignoring the water above the gauge fluid: use $SG_g - 1$, not $SG_g$.
Leaving the manometer reading in inches.
Dropping the 2 under the square root.

A.statement: The flow leaving a booster pump station is metered by a sharp-edged orifice plate with a 4-in. bore, mounted in the horizontal 8-in. discharge line. The differential pressure across the plate is 5.0 psi, and the meter coefficient $C$ (which already includes contraction, velocity and approach effects) is 0.62. With $\gamma_w = 62.4\ \text{lbf/ft}^3$, the discharge is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Divides 5.0 psi by 62.4 without converting to lbf/ft² (×144), so the head is 144 times too small.
Drops the 2 in $\sqrt{2g\,\Delta h}$.
Leaves out the meter coefficient, which gives the ideal flow.
A.eli5: Squeezing the flow through a smaller hole speeds it up and drops the pressure. The pressure drop tells you how fast the water goes through the hole; the coefficient corrects the ideal answer to what a real plate passes.
A.hint: Turn the pressure drop into feet of water, then $Q = C A_0\sqrt{2g\,\Delta h}$ with $A_0$ the bore area.

steps.text: Pressure drop as a head of water.
Area of the 4-in. bore.
Discharge through the orifice meter (horizontal, so no elevation term).

traps: Forgetting that 1 psi is 144 lbf/ft².
Using the pipe area instead of the orifice bore area.
Applying an approach-velocity correction a second time when $C$ already includes it.

A.statement: An open wash-water tank at a concrete batch plant drains through a 50-mm sharp-edged orifice in its side wall. The water surface is held 4.5 m above the center of the orifice, and the orifice has a discharge coefficient of 0.61. The discharge is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Ideal flow: leaves out the discharge coefficient.
Divides by 0.61 instead of multiplying. A real orifice passes less than the ideal flow, never more.
Uses $\pi(0.050)^2$, treating the 50 mm diameter as a radius, which makes the area four times too large.
A.eli5: Water at the hole falls as if it had dropped from the surface, so its speed is $\sqrt{2gh}$. Multiply by the hole's area for the ideal flow, then by 0.61 because a sharp-edged jet necks down and loses a little speed.
A.hint: Torricelli: $v = \sqrt{2gh}$, and $Q = C A_0 \sqrt{2gh}$ with $h$ to the orifice center.

steps.text: Ideal jet velocity from the head on the orifice.
Orifice area.
Discharge with the coefficient.

traps: Leaving out the discharge coefficient, or dividing by it.
Using the diameter as a radius in the area.

A.statement: A 300-mm water transmission main leaves a reservoir whose surface is at El. 120.0 m and crosses a ridge, where the pipe centerline reaches El. 115.0 m. The main carries 0.15 m³/s, and the head loss from the reservoir to the summit is 2.4 m. With $\gamma = 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3$, the gauge pressure in the pipe at the summit is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Uses $v^2/g$ for the velocity head, dropping the 1/2, so 0.46 m is taken off instead of 0.23 m.
Leaves out the velocity head in the pipe. At the reservoir surface the water is still, but in the pipe it is moving at 2.12 m/s.
Leaves out the 2.4 m head loss, treating the flow as frictionless (Bernoulli without losses).
A.eli5: Start with 5 m of height to spend between the reservoir surface and the summit. Friction uses 2.4 m of it and getting the water moving uses a little more. Whatever is left over shows up as pressure.
A.hint: Write the energy equation from the reservoir surface (pressure 0, velocity 0) to the summit, including the head loss and the velocity head in the pipe.

steps.text: Velocity in the main and its velocity head.
Energy equation from the reservoir surface (1) to the summit (2).
Solve for the pressure head and the pressure.

traps: Forgetting the velocity head in the pipe at the summit.
Dropping the 1/2 in $v^2/2g$.
Using Bernoulli without the head loss when a loss is given.

A.statement: On a hydraulics lab test rig, a 60-mm water jet traveling at 22 m/s is turned 120° from its original direction by a stationary curved deflector blade, as shown (plan view, horizontal plane). Friction on the blade is negligible, so the jet keeps its speed. With $\rho = 1{,}000\ \text{kg/m}^3$, the magnitude of the total force the water exerts on the blade is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Gives only the y component, $\rho Q v \sin 120°$.
Uses $(1 + \cos 120°)$ for the x change in velocity, which makes the x component too small; the resultant then equals just $\rho Q v$.
Gives only the x component, $\rho Q v(1 - \cos 120°)$, and forgets the y component.
A.eli5: The blade has to stop the water moving forward, send it partly backward, and give it a sideways push. The force is the mass of water per second times how much its velocity changes. Find the change along x and along y, then combine them.
A.hint: Use $-F_x = \rho Q(v_2\cos\alpha - v_1)$ and $F_y = \rho Q v_2\sin\alpha$ with $v_2 = v_1$ and $\alpha = 120°$.

steps.text: Jet area, flow and momentum flux.
x component: the velocity goes from $+v$ to $v\cos 120° = -0.5v$.
y component.
Resultant on the blade.

traps: Sign of $\cos 120°$: it is negative, so the x change is $1.5v$, more than a full stop.
Reporting one component instead of the resultant.

B.statement: A closed-loop test rig for a booster pump is filled with a coolant made by blending 30 L of ethylene glycol (SG = 1.11) with 70 L of water. Assume the two volumes simply add. The density of the coolant is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Correct: the mass is $30(1.11) + 70(1.00) = 103.3\ \text{kg}$ in $100\ \text{L}$, so $SG = 1.033$ and $\rho = 1{,}033\ \text{kg/m}^3$.
Takes the plain average of the two specific gravities, $(1.11 + 1.00)/2 = 1.055$, as if the blend were half and half. The average must be weighted by volume.
Weights the average the wrong way round: 70 parts glycol and 30 parts water, $0.70(1.11) + 0.30(1.00) = 1.077$.
Reports the density of pure glycol, $1.11 \times 1{,}000$, and ignores the water in the blend.
B.eli5: Weigh what goes in. 30 liters of glycol weigh 1.11 kg each, 70 liters of water weigh 1 kg each, so 100 liters of blend weigh 103.3 kg. That is 1.033 kg per liter, or 1,033 kg per cubic meter.
B.hint: Add the masses of the two liquids and divide by the total volume.

steps.text: Mass of each liquid from its volume and specific gravity (1 L of water has a mass of 1 kg).
Divide by the total volume, 100 L, to get the specific gravity of the blend.
Convert to density.

traps: Averaging the specific gravities without weighting them by volume.
Swapping the weights between the two liquids.

B.statement: A compressor fills the receiver tank that supplies the air tools on a bridge repainting job. The tank gauge reads 600 kPa, the air in the tank is at 25°C, and atmospheric pressure is 101.3 kPa. Treating air as an ideal gas with $R = 287\ \text{J/(kg·K)}$, the density of the air in the tank is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Uses the gauge pressure, 600 kPa, in the ideal gas law. The law needs absolute pressure: add the atmosphere.
Correct: $\rho = P/(RT) = 701{,}300/(287 \times 298.15) = 8.20\ \text{kg/m}^3$, with absolute pressure and absolute temperature.
Uses gauge pressure and the temperature in °C (25 instead of 298.15 K). Both must be absolute.
Uses absolute pressure but the temperature in °C. At 25 "degrees" the gas looks about twelve times denser than it is.
B.eli5: The ideal gas law only works with "real zero" scales. Pressure has to count from a perfect vacuum, so add the atmosphere to the gauge reading. Temperature has to count from absolute zero, so add 273.15 to the Celsius value. Then density is pressure over R times temperature.
B.hint: In $P = \rho R T$, both $P$ and $T$ are absolute.

steps.text: Absolute pressure is gauge plus atmospheric.
Absolute temperature.
Solve the ideal gas law for density.

traps: Putting the gauge pressure into the ideal gas law.
Using degrees Celsius instead of kelvin.

B.statement: The 80-mm shaft of a lift station pump turns at 1,200 rpm inside a sleeve bearing 120 mm long, as shown. The diametral clearance between the shaft and the sleeve is 0.20 mm and is filled with oil of dynamic viscosity $\mu = 0.12\ \text{Pa·s}$. Assuming a linear velocity profile across the oil film, the torque needed to overcome viscous drag in the bearing is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Converts 1,200 rpm to 20 rev/s and uses that as the angular speed, forgetting the factor of $2\pi$ rad per revolution. The surface speed comes out 0.80 m/s instead of 5.03 m/s.
Uses the diametral clearance, 0.20 mm, as the film thickness. The film on each side is half of it, 0.10 mm, so the shear stress is twice as large.
Correct: $v = \omega r = 125.7(0.040) = 5.03\ \text{m/s}$, $\tau = \mu v/\delta = 6{,}032\ \text{Pa}$, $F = \tau(\pi D L) = 181.9\ \text{N}$ and $T = F r = 7.28\ \text{N·m}$.
Multiplies the drag force by the shaft diameter instead of the radius. The force acts at the surface of the shaft, one radius from its axis.
B.eli5: The shaft surface slides past the sleeve, and the thin oil layer between them resists that sliding. Find how fast the surface moves, divide by the oil thickness and multiply by the viscosity to get the drag per square meter. Multiply by the area of the oil layer to get the drag force, and by the shaft radius to get the twisting effort.
B.hint: Shear stress is $\mu v/\delta$ with $v$ the surface speed and $\delta$ the film thickness on one side. Torque is force times radius.

steps.text: Angular speed and surface speed of the shaft.
The film thickness is half the diametral clearance.
Shear stress in the film, with a linear velocity profile.
Drag force over the wetted area of the shaft.
Torque about the shaft axis.

traps: Using the diametral clearance as the film thickness.
Leaving out $2\pi$ when converting rpm to rad/s.
Using the diameter as the moment arm.

B.statement: A closed steel tank at a treatment plant holds 2.0 m of water with a 1.5-m layer of oil (SG = 0.85) floating on it and air above, as shown. A gauge at the bottom of the tank reads 45.0 kPa. Using $\gamma_w = 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3$, the gauge pressure of the air above the oil is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Treats the oil layer as water, subtracting $9.81(3.5) = 34.3\ \text{kPa}$. The oil is lighter, so it accounts for less pressure.
Swaps the layer thicknesses, giving the oil 2.0 m and the water 1.5 m.
Adds the liquid columns to the bottom reading instead of subtracting them. Pressure falls going up from the gauge to the air.
B.eli5: The bottom gauge feels the air pushing down plus the weight of both liquid layers. Take away what the water layer adds and what the oil layer adds, and what is left is the push from the air.
B.hint: Start at the gauge and climb up through each layer, subtracting $\gamma h$ for each one.

steps.text: Pressure added by each liquid layer.
The bottom reading is the air pressure plus both layers, so subtract them.

traps: Using the specific weight of water for the oil layer.
Adding the columns when moving upward.

B.statement: An inverted U-tube manometer joins two water pipes, A and B, as shown. The bend at the top of the manometer holds oil of SG 0.80. Measured up from the center of pipe A, the oil-water interface in the leg from A is at 1.20 m, the center of pipe B is at 0.30 m, and the oil-water interface in the leg from B is at 0.95 m. Using $\gamma_w = 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3$, the pressure difference $p_A - p_B$ is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Right size, wrong sign: adds $\gamma h$ going up and subtracts it going down. Pressure falls as you rise through a fluid.
Measures the water column in the B leg from the interface down to the level of A instead of to the center of B (0.95 m instead of 0.65 m), as if the pipes were at the same elevation.
Leaves out the 0.25-m oil column between the two interfaces, as if the top of the U-tube held air.
B.eli5: Walk through the tube from A to B. Going up the water in A's leg, pressure drops. Going down through the short oil column, it rises a little. Going down the water in B's leg to the center of B, it rises again. Add those steps and you have how much more pressure A has than B.
B.hint: Write $p_A$, then add $\gamma h$ for every step down and subtract it for every step up until you reach the center of B.

steps.text: Up the water in the A leg, from the center of A to its interface.
Down through the oil from 1.20 m to 0.95 m.
Down the water in the B leg from 0.95 m to the center of B at 0.30 m.
This equals $p_B$. Solve for the difference.

traps: Ignoring that pipe B sits higher than pipe A.
Mixing up which direction adds pressure.
Forgetting the oil column, or treating it as water.

B.statement: A cylindrical steel navigation buoy is 1.2 m in diameter and 2.0 m tall and has a mass of 900 kg. It floats upright in seawater ($\rho = 1{,}025\ \text{kg/m}^3$), and its mooring chain pulls straight down on the center of its base with a force of 2.0 kN, as shown. The draft of the buoy (the depth of its base below the water surface) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Uses the diameter, 1.2 m, as the radius in $\pi r^2$, so the area is four times too large.
Subtracts the chain pull from the weight. The chain pulls down, the same way as gravity, so it adds to the load the water must hold up.
Ignores the chain and floats the buoy on its own weight.
Correct: buoyancy must carry $8.83 + 2.0 = 10.83\ \text{kN}$, and each meter of draft displaces $1{,}025(9.81)(1.131) = 11.37\ \text{kN}$, so $d = 0.952\ \text{m}$.
B.eli5: The water has to hold up the buoy and the chain tugging it down. Every meter the buoy sinks pushes aside one circle-of-water-meter, which weighs a fixed amount. Divide the total downward load by that weight per meter and you get how deep it sits.
B.hint: At equilibrium, buoyancy equals weight plus chain pull. Buoyancy is $\rho g A d$.

steps.text: Weight of the buoy and the total downward load.
Plan area of the buoy.
Buoyancy equals the downward load (Archimedes).
Check: 0.952 m is less than the 2.0-m height, so the buoy floats.

traps: Leaving out the chain pull, or subtracting it.
Using the diameter in place of the radius for the area.
Using fresh water instead of seawater.

B.statement: The lower corner of a tank is closed by a gate shaped as a quarter of a circular cylinder, with a radius of 1.5 m and a length of 4 m perpendicular to the page, as shown. The center of the arc, O, is level with the top edge of the gate, A, and the water surface is 1.0 m above A. Behind the gate is a dry recess at atmospheric pressure. Using $\gamma_w = 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3$, the magnitude of the resultant hydrostatic force on the gate is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Gives only the horizontal component, 103 kN. The water above the gate also pushes it down, and that component is the larger one.
Takes the vertical component as the weight of the quarter circle of water only, 69.3 kN, and forgets the 1.0-m layer of water above the top of the gate.
Correct: $F_H = 103.0\ \text{kN}$ and $F_V = 128.2\ \text{kN}$, so $F = \sqrt{103.0^2 + 128.2^2} = 164\ \text{kN}$.
Takes the vertical component as the weight of a full 1.5 m by 2.5 m block of water, 147.2 kN, as if the gate were flat. The curve leaves out the corner, so less water sits above it.
B.eli5: Split the push on the curved gate into a sideways part and a downward part. The sideways part is the same as on a flat wall as tall as the gate. The downward part is just the weight of the water sitting right above the curve, up to the surface. Combine the two like the sides of a right triangle.
B.hint: Horizontal: the force on the vertical projection of the gate. Vertical: the weight of the water directly above the curved surface, up to the free surface.

steps.text: Horizontal component: force on the vertical projection, 1.5 m tall and 4 m long, with its centroid $1.0 + 0.75 = 1.75\ \text{m}$ deep.
Water directly above the curve, per meter of length: the 1.0-m layer over the gate plus the quarter circle between the arc and the level of A.
Vertical component is the weight of that water.
Combine the components.

traps: Reporting one component instead of the resultant.
Forgetting the water above the top of the gate in the vertical component.
Adding the components directly instead of as vectors.

B.statement: A pitot-static probe sits on the centerline of a 24-in. pump discharge pipe carrying water ($\rho = 1.94\ \text{slug/ft}^3$). The differential pressure transducer connected to the probe reads 0.80 psi, as shown. The velocity of the water at the probe is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Leaves the pressure in psi instead of converting to lbf/ft² (times 144).
Divides by the specific weight, 62.4 lbf/ft³, where the formula needs the mass density, 1.94 slug/ft³.
Forgets the 2 in $v = \sqrt{2\Delta p/\rho}$, which comes from the 1/2 in the kinetic energy term.
Correct: $\Delta p = 0.80(144) = 115.2\ \text{lbf/ft}^2$ and $v = \sqrt{2(115.2)/1.94} = 10.9\ \text{ft/sec}$.
B.eli5: The nose of the probe stops the water dead, so the pressure there is a bit higher than the pressure felt by the side holes. That extra pressure is the moving water's energy. Set it equal to one half times density times speed squared and solve for the speed.
B.hint: Stagnation minus static pressure equals $\rho v^2/2$. Work in lbf/ft² and slug/ft³.

steps.text: Convert the reading to lbf/ft².
Solve the stagnation pressure equation for velocity.

traps: Skipping the psi to lbf/ft² conversion.
Using specific weight where mass density belongs.

B.statement: A horizontal venturi meter in a raw-water line has an 8-in. inlet and a 6-in. throat. Pressure gauges read 38.0 psi at the inlet and 35.5 psi at the throat, as shown, and the coefficient of velocity is 0.98. The flow rate is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Leaves out the approach factor $1/\sqrt{1 - (A_2/A_1)^2}$, treating the water as if it entered the meter at rest.
Uses $1 - (A_2/A_1)$ instead of $1 - (A_2/A_1)^2$ under the root, which is the same as using the diameter ratio squared instead of to the fourth power.
Multiplies by the inlet area instead of the throat area.
B.eli5: The water speeds up in the narrow throat, and that costs it pressure. The pressure drop tells you how much faster it goes in the throat than at the inlet. A small correction accounts for the water already moving at the inlet, and the coefficient trims off a little for friction. Throat speed times throat area is the flow.
B.hint: Use the handbook venturi equation with the throat area, $A_2$, and the area ratio squared in the root.

steps.text: Pressure drop as head of water.
Areas and their ratio.
Venturi equation, with $z_1 = z_2$.
Evaluate.

traps: Dropping the approach factor.
Using the inlet area where the throat area belongs.
Forgetting to convert psi to lbf/ft² before dividing by 62.4.

B.statement: A water line runs downhill from a storage tank to a treatment plant, as shown. At point 1 the pipe is 12 in. in diameter and the pressure is 30 psi. At point 2, 10 ft lower and past a reducer, the pipe is 8 in. in diameter. The flow is 6 ft³/sec. Neglecting head loss, the pressure at point 2 is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Subtracts the 10-ft drop instead of adding it. Point 2 is lower, so it gains pressure from the elevation change.
Leaves out the elevation change and accounts only for the speed-up in the smaller pipe.
Uses $v^2/g$ instead of $v^2/2g$ for the velocity heads, so the speed-up costs twice the pressure it should.
B.eli5: The water gains pressure because it drops 10 ft, and loses some because it has to speed up to squeeze through the smaller pipe. Bernoulli keeps the books: pressure head plus elevation plus speed head stays the same from 1 to 2.
B.hint: Find both velocities from $Q = Av$, then write Bernoulli from 1 to 2 with the datum at point 2.

steps.text: Velocities from continuity.
Velocity heads.
Pressure head at 1.
Bernoulli with the datum at point 2, so $z_1 = 10$ ft and $z_2 = 0$.
Back to psi.

traps: Getting the sign of the elevation change wrong.
Dropping the 2 in $v^2/2g$.
Mixing psi and lbf/ft² in the same equation.

B.statement: A horizontal 100-mm fire line ends in a nozzle bolted to its flange, as shown. The nozzle discharges a 40-mm free jet of water ($\rho = 1{,}000\ \text{kg/m}^3$) to the atmosphere at $0.020\ \text{m}^3\text{/s}$. Neglecting friction and the weight of the water, the total force the flange bolts must carry is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Uses only the change in momentum flux, $\rho Q(v_2 - v_1)$, and leaves out the pressure force at the flange.
Correct: $p_1 = 123.4\ \text{kPa}$ from Bernoulli, $p_1 A_1 = 969\ \text{N}$, and the water pushes the nozzle downstream with $969 - 267 = 702\ \text{N}$.
Uses only the pressure force at the flange, $p_1 A_1$, and forgets that part of it goes into speeding up the water.

Adds the momentum term to the pressure force instead of subtracting it. The net forward force on the water is only $\rho Q(v_2 - v_1) = 267\ \text{N}$, so the nozzle holds it back with $969 - 267 = 702\ \text{N}$, not $969 + 267$.
B.eli5: The water arrives at the flange under pressure and leaves the tip much faster at zero pressure. The pressure at the flange pushes the water and the nozzle forward. Some of that push is used up speeding the water up; the rest shoves the nozzle off the pipe, and the bolts hold it back.
B.hint: Find $p_1$ from Bernoulli between the flange and the jet. Then apply impulse-momentum to the water inside the nozzle: $p_1 A_1 - F = \rho Q(v_2 - v_1)$.

steps.text: Areas and velocities.
Pressure at the flange from Bernoulli, with $p_2 = 0$ in the free jet and no elevation change.
Pressure force at the flange and momentum change.
Impulse-momentum on the water in the nozzle, with $F$ the force of the nozzle on the water (taken upstream).
steps.latex: p_1 A_1 - F = \rho Q(v_2 - v_1) \Rightarrow F = 969 - 267 = 702\ \text{N}

steps.text: The water pushes the nozzle downstream with an equal and opposite 702 N, which the bolts must hold.

B.handbookFormula: \Sigma F = Q\rho(v_2 - v_1),\quad P_1A_1 - P_2A_2 - F_x = Q\rho(v_2 - v_1)
traps: Forgetting the pressure force at the flange.
Taking the pressure force alone.
Getting the sign of the momentum term wrong.

A.statement: The three sides of the triangular lot ABC shown were taped in the field. The interior angle at corner B is most nearly:
choiceNotes: This is the angle at A: it uses BC (365.20 ft) as the side opposite the angle instead of AC.
This is the angle at C: it uses AB (412.50 ft) as the side opposite the angle instead of AC.
The acute supplement of the right answer. It comes from a sign slip in the law of cosines, or from the law of sines, which cannot tell an obtuse angle from its supplement.
Correct: AC is the side opposite B, so $\cos B = (a^2 + c^2 - b^2)/(2ac) = -0.1813$, and B is obtuse.
A.eli5: You know all three sides and want one corner. The law of cosines turns three sides into any angle, as long as the side you subtract is the one across from the corner you want. Across from B is the long side AC. Because AC is so long, the cosine comes out negative, which means B is wider than a right angle.
A.hint: Which side is across from corner B? That is the side you subtract in the law of cosines.

steps.text: Name the sides by the corner they face: a = BC = 365.20 ft, b = AC = 598.40 ft (opposite B), c = AB = 412.50 ft.
Law of cosines solved for B:
Evaluate:
A negative cosine means an obtuse angle:

B.statement: A surveyor ties a subdivision to the state plane coordinate system and has to relate grid values to what is measured on the ground. Which of the following statements is true?

choices.text: The grid scale factor is exactly 1.0000 at every point in a zone.
Grid north and true north point the same way at every point in a zone.
A Lambert conformal conic projection is used for zones that run east to west.
The elevation factor alone turns a ground distance into a grid distance.

choiceNotes: False: a flat grid cannot match a curved earth everywhere. The scale factor is below 1 near the middle of a zone and above 1 near its edges.
False: grid north is parallel to the central meridian everywhere, while true north points to the pole, so the two differ by the convergence angle everywhere off the central meridian.

Correct: a cone touches the earth along lines of latitude, so its distortion is smallest along an east-west band, which suits states like Tennessee. North-south zones use a transverse Mercator projection.
False: the grid distance needs the combined factor, which is the elevation (sea level) factor times the grid scale factor.
B.eli5: A state plane grid is a flat map of a curved earth, and every flat map has to stretch somewhere. A cone-shaped (Lambert) map fits well along a wide east-west strip, and a cylinder-shaped (transverse Mercator) map fits well along a tall north-south strip. That is why the projection is picked by the shape of the zone.
B.hint: Think about which shape (cone or cylinder) hugs the earth along an east-west band.

steps.text: Projections are chosen to keep distortion small over the zone. A cone tangent or secant along parallels of latitude (Lambert conformal conic) keeps the scale factor near 1 over an east-west band; a transverse Mercator cylinder does so over a north-south band.
The scale factor varies across a zone, grid north departs from true north away from the central meridian (convergence), and ground-to-grid needs the combined factor.

traps: The scale factor is not 1 everywhere; it changes with distance from the central meridian or the standard parallels.
Ground to grid uses both factors, elevation and scale.

A.statement: The hyetograph shown is for a 5-hour storm on a small rural watershed. Stream gauging shows the storm produced 1.8 in. of direct runoff over the watershed. The $\phi$-index (in./hr) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Spreads the 2.5 in. of loss evenly over all 5 hours, but hours 1 and 5 have less rain than that rate, so the loss cannot be uniform there.

Divides the total loss of 2.5 in. by the 3 runoff-producing hours, forgetting that all the rain in hours 1 and 5 is lost too.
A.eli5: The phi-index is a flat infiltration rate: every hour the ground soaks up phi inches, and only rain above that line runs off. Hours with less rain than phi lose all of it, so they cannot be part of the runoff count. Guess which hours are above the line, solve for phi from those hours only, then check that the left-out hours really are below it.
A.hint: Runoff equals the sum of (rain minus phi) over only the hours whose rain is greater than phi.

traps: Dividing total loss by the full storm duration; hours with rain below phi lose only what fell.
Forgetting to check that every excluded hour is really below phi and every included hour above it.

The free chlorine residual at the outlet, measured during peak hourly flow, is 1.2 mg/L. Estimating $t_{10}$ from the baffling factor, the calculated CT (mg·min/L) is most nearly:

the overflow rate at which the sedimentation basins should be operated
how long the filters can run before they must be backwashed
the coagulant dose and pH that give the best floc and the clearest settled water

choiceNotes: Confuses the jar test with a chlorine demand test; chlorine dosing is set from demand and residual measurements.

Correct: side-by-side jars with different coagulant doses (and pH) are mixed, flocculated and settled to find the most effective dose.

A.handbookFormula: No equation: jar test = bench test for optimum coagulant dose and pH

Converting to a 2-hour unit hydrograph by lagging, the peak direct runoff from the design storm (cfs) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Stops at the peak of the 2-hour unit hydrograph and never multiplies by the 1.8 in. of excess.

choiceNotes: Uses the hydraulic jump (momentum) equation, which links sequent depths, not the energy equation that links alternate depths across a gate.
Correct: q = 15 cfs/ft, E = 5.0 + 0.14 = 5.14 ft, and the supercritical depth with the same specific energy is 0.91 ft.

Compute the upstream energy, then try small depths until the downstream energy matches.

B.statement: A water utility samples its distribution system every week for total coliform bacteria. Coliforms are tested for mainly because they:

choices.text: cause most of the waterborne illness traced to treated public supplies
use up dissolved oxygen and so measure the organic strength of the water
pass through disinfection but not filtration, so they test the filters
come from the same source as fecal pathogens, so they signal contamination

choiceNotes: Most coliforms are harmless; the illness comes from pathogens that are too varied and too few to test for one by one.
That describes the BOD test, not a bacteriological test.
Coliforms are readily killed by chlorine, which is why their presence after disinfection is a warning sign.
Correct: coliforms are an indicator group; they are plentiful in feces and easy to culture, so finding them means pathogens may be present.
B.eli5: Testing water for every germ that can make people sick would be slow and expensive, and most of them are rare. Coliform bacteria live in large numbers in human and animal waste and are easy to grow in a lab. If they show up in the water, waste may have got in, and the dangerous germs that travel with waste may be there too.
B.hint: Think of coliforms as an indicator, not as the hazard itself.

steps.text: Pathogens are many, varied and usually few in number, so testing for each is impractical.
steps.latex: \text{test for an indicator, not each pathogen}

steps.text: Coliforms are abundant in fecal matter, simple to culture and killed by disinfection, so a positive sample signals possible fecal contamination or a failure in treatment or the distribution system.

B.handbookFormula: \text{Indicator organism: total coliform (fecal coliform, } E.\ coli\text{)}
traps: Thinking coliforms themselves are the main disease agents.
Confusing a bacteriological test with an oxygen-demand test.

A.topic: Analysis of statically determinate trusses, beams and frames
A.statement: The pedestrian bridge truss shown is a Warren truss with no verticals. It carries 18 kips at each of joints L1, L2 and L3 and is supported by a pin at L0 and a roller at L4. The force in diagonal U2L2 (kips) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: This is the shear in the panel (27 - 18 = 9 kips), not the member force: the diagonal must carry it with only its vertical component.
Right size, wrong sense. With positive shear in the left half, a diagonal that slopes down toward midspan is pulled, not pushed.
Correct: the panel shear of 9 kips equals the vertical component of the diagonal, 0.8F, so F = 11.25 kips, in tension.
Divides the shear by the horizontal ratio (6/10 = 0.6) instead of the vertical ratio (8/10 = 0.8).
A.eli5: Cut the truss just left of L2 and look at the left piece. The support pushes up 27 kips and the load at L1 pushes down 18, so 9 kips of "up" is left over. The only cut member that can push or pull up and down is the diagonal, and since it leans at 8 up for every 10 along, it has to carry 9 / 0.8 = 11.25 kips to supply 9 kips of vertical pull.
A.hint: Cut through U2U3, U2L2 and L1L2 and sum vertical forces on the left piece; the two chords are horizontal.

steps.text: Reactions by symmetry: the three 18-kip loads are symmetric, so each support takes half.
Diagonal geometry: it runs 6 ft across and 8 ft down, so its length is 10 ft and its vertical component is 8/10 of its force.

Solve. A positive answer means tension.

traps: Stopping at the panel shear (9 kips) and forgetting the diagonal carries it at a slope.

A.topic: Analysis of statically determinate trusses, beams and frames
A.statement: A parking-deck beam has an internal hinge at C, as shown. Span C-D carries a uniform load of 2 kips/ft; spans A-B and B-C are unloaded (neglect self-weight). The vertical reaction at A (kips) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Correct: span C-D hands 15 kips down to the overhang at C; moments about B give R_A = -15(5)/20 = -3.75 kips, so A holds the beam down.
Right size but the wrong direction: the load at the overhang tip lifts A, so A must pull down.
Puts the whole 30 kips of load at the hinge instead of the 15 kips the drop-in span delivers there.
This is the reaction at B (15 + 3.75), not at A.
A.eli5: The short span C-D is like a plank resting on a shelf at C and a post at D. It hands half its load, 15 kips, to the tip of the overhang at C. That tip load sits beyond support B, so the beam A-B-C acts like a see-saw over B: pushing down at C makes A want to rise, and A has to hold it down with 15 x 5 / 20 = 3.75 kips.
A.hint: Solve the drop-in span C-D first: a hinge carries shear but no moment.

steps.text: Free body C-D: the hinge cannot carry moment, so C-D is a simple span. Its total load is 2(15) = 30 kips, split equally.
Free body A-B-C: the hinge force of 15 kips acts down at C, 5 ft beyond B. Take moments about B (R_A positive up).
Solve. The negative sign means the reaction acts downward.
Check: R_B = 15 + 3.75 = 18.75 kips upward, and 18.75 - 3.75 = 15 kips balances the hinge force.

traps: Treating the beam as one rigid piece and putting the full 30 kips at C.
Assuming every reaction points up; an overhang load lifts the far support.
Reporting R_B instead of R_A.

A.topic: Analysis of statically determinate trusses, beams and frames
A.statement: A salt-storage shed is framed with the three-hinged frame shown: pinned bases A and E, rigid knees B and D, and a hinge C at midspan of the girder. The girder carries a uniform load of 2 kips/ft over its full length. The horizontal reaction at A (kips) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Halves the thrust as if the two bases shared it. Each base carries the full horizontal thrust H = wL^2/8h = 18.75 kips, equal and opposite.
Correct: with V_A = 30 kips, moments about the hinge C on the left half give 12H = 30(15) - 30(7.5), so H = 18.75 kips.

Forgets to subtract the moment of the load on the left half about C (uses 30 x 15 / 12).
A.eli5: The two halves of the frame lean on each other at the hinge C, and that makes the feet want to slide outward. The hinge cannot hold a bending moment, so on the left half the turning effect of the upward reaction about C must be cancelled by the load on that half plus a sideways push at the foot. Whatever is left over, divided by the 12 ft height, is that push.
A.hint: Get the vertical reaction from symmetry, then take moments about hinge C using only the left half.

Free body of the left half (A-B-C). The hinge has zero moment, so sum moments about C. The 15 ft of load on that half (30 kips) acts 7.5 ft from C.
Solve for the horizontal reaction.
Same result from the closed form for a uniformly loaded three-hinged frame with the hinge at midspan.

traps: Leaving out the load on the left half when taking moments about C.
Answering with the vertical reaction.

Splitting the thrust between the two bases.
