Using the total-load limit L/240 for a live-load check.
Forgetting the factor 5.

A.topic: Deflection of statically determinate beams, trusses and frames
A.statement: The steel roof truss shown ($E = 29{,}000 \text{ ksi}$) carries 30 kips at apex B. Member areas are marked on the figure. Using the unit load method, the vertical deflection of joint B (in.) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Gives the compression members a positive f while keeping their F negative, so their terms cancel the chord instead of adding to it.
Counts only the tension chord AC and leaves out the two sloping members.
Adds FL/AE for every member without multiplying by the unit-load force f.
A.eli5: Each member stretches or shortens a little under the real load. To find how much the apex drops, you ask: if I pushed down on B with a 1-kip load, how hard would each member work? Multiply each member's real stretch by that "how hard" number and add them up. Because every number here is proportional to the same apex load, the sloping members and the chord all add in the same direction.
A.hint: Find the real forces F from 30 kips at B, the virtual forces f from 1 kip at B, then sum $FfL/AE$ with lengths in inches.

steps.text: Geometry: half-span 12 ft and height 9 ft give sloping members 15 ft long (a 3-4-5 triangle). Reactions are 15 kips each.
steps.latex: L_{AB} = L_{BC} = 15 \text{ ft} = 180 \text{ in.},\; L_{AC} = 288 \text{ in.}

steps.text: Real forces at joint A: the vertical component of AB balances the 15-kip reaction, and AC balances its horizontal component.
Virtual forces from 1 kip down at B are the real forces divided by 30.
Sum FfL/A for the three members.
Divide by E.

traps: Mixing signs: a compression member has negative F and negative f, so its product is positive.
Leaving the member lengths in feet while E is in ksi.
Using one area for all three members.

A.statement: A steel strut in a pipe rack ($E = 29{,}000 \text{ ksi}$, proportional limit 30 ksi, $r = 1.20 \text{ in.}$) is fixed at its base and pinned at its top. Using the theoretical effective-length factor, the shortest length (ft) for which Euler's formula is valid is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Leaves the $\pi$ out of the limiting slenderness ($\sqrt{E/\sigma}$ alone).
Multiplies the limiting $KL/r$ by K instead of dividing by it.
Uses K = 1.0 (pinned-pinned) and ignores the fixed base.
A.eli5: Euler's formula only works while the steel is still springy, below its proportional limit. That sets a minimum slenderness. A fixed base makes the strut behave like a shorter one (K = 0.7), so the real strut has to be longer than a pin-ended one to reach that slenderness.
A.hint: Set the Euler stress equal to the proportional limit and solve for KL/r.

steps.text: Euler is valid while the critical stress does not exceed the proportional limit.
Limiting slenderness.
Fixed-pinned: theoretical K = 0.7. Solve for L.

traps: Using K = 1.0 for every column.
Multiplying by K instead of dividing when solving for L.
Mixing the theoretical K (0.7) with the AISC-recommended design value (0.80) when the question asks for the theoretical one.

A.topic: Determinacy and stability of beams, trusses and frames
A.statement: The canopy frame shown has a fixed base at A, a pinned base at D, rigid knees at B and C, and an internal hinge at E in the girder. The frame is best classified as:

choices.text: Stable and indeterminate to the first degree
Stable and indeterminate to the second degree

choiceNotes: Counts the pin at D as one reaction (r = 4), which would make 3m + r equal 3j + c.
Correct: m = 4, j = 5, r = 3 + 2 = 5, c = 1, so 3m + r = 17 against 3j + c = 16, one more unknown than equations.
Ignores the hinge (c = 0), which leaves the fixed-pinned portal two degrees indeterminate.
A single hinge in the girder of a frame with a fixed base and a pinned base does not form a mechanism; the frame is stable.
A.eli5: Count the unknowns and the equations. The fixed base gives 3 unknowns and the pin gives 2, so 5 outside unknowns; a frame has 3 equations, and the hinge adds one more (zero moment there), so 4. Five unknowns, four equations: one too many, so the frame is one degree indeterminate.
A.hint: Use the Handbook plane-frame test 3m + r versus 3j + c, with the hinge as a joint between two members.

steps.text: Count members and joints, treating the hinge E as a joint: members AB, BE, EC, CD; joints A, B, E, C, D.
Reactions: fixed base 3, pin 2. Condition equations: one hinge joining two members.
Compare.

traps: Giving a pin one reaction instead of two.
Forgetting the condition equation at the hinge.
Using the truss test m + r versus 2j on a frame.

A.statement: A continuous floor beam of constant EI spans two equal 20-ft spans on three supports and carries a uniform load of 3 kips/ft over its full length, as shown. The reaction at the interior support B (kips) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: This is an end reaction, $3wL/8$ per span, not the interior one.
Uses one span (20 ft) as L in $5wL/8$; the Handbook case uses the full length between A and C.
Treats the beam as two simple spans (half of each span to B). Continuity draws more load to the middle support.
Correct: remove B, match deflections: $B_y = 5wL/8$ with L = 40 ft, so $B_y = 5(3)(40)/8 = 75$ kips.
A.eli5: If the middle support were gone, the 40-ft beam would sag in the middle. The middle support has to push up just hard enough to undo that sag. The Handbook does this exact case: the push is 5/8 of w times the whole length, which is more than the 60 kips you would get by pretending the two spans are separate.
A.hint: Treat B as the redundant: the sag of a 40-ft simple beam under w must be cancelled by $B_y L^3/48EI$.

steps.text: Remove B. Midspan deflection of the 40-ft simple beam under w.
Deflection at midspan from a unit upward force at B.
Compatibility: the net deflection at B is zero.
Evaluate with the full length L = 40 ft.

traps: Using one span as L in the Handbook case.
Splitting load to the supports as if the spans were simple (60 kips at B).
Answering with an end reaction.

A.topic: Loads, load combinations and load paths
A.statement: The office floor in the framing plan shown has a dead load of 80 psf (including framing) and a live load of 50 psf. Ignoring live load reduction, the factored axial load (kips) that column B2 receives from this floor under the LRFD combination 1.2D + 1.6L is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Uses half a bay (375 ft²), the tributary area of an edge column, not an interior one.
Uses 1.4D only, which does not govern when there is live load of this size.
Leaves the loads unfactored (D + L).
Correct: tributary area = 25 x 30 = 750 ft², D = 60 kips, L = 37.5 kips, so 1.2(60) + 1.6(37.5) = 132 kips.
A.eli5: An interior column holds up the floor halfway to each neighbouring column in every direction. That is a patch one bay wide by one bay deep, 25 ft by 30 ft. Multiply the patch area by each pressure, then apply the load factors.
A.hint: An interior column's tributary area reaches halfway to the next column line on all four sides.

steps.text: Tributary area of interior column B2: half a bay each side in both directions.
Service loads on the column.
Factored load.

traps: Using an edge or corner column's tributary area for an interior column.
Forgetting to factor the loads.
Mixing psf and kips (divide by 1,000).

A.topic: Loads, load combinations and load paths
A.statement: A top-story column of an auditorium (an area of public assembly) has these nominal axial compression loads: dead D = 40 kips, floor live L = 25 kips, roof live Lr = 10 kips, and wind W = 30 kips (compression in this column; there is no snow, rain or earthquake load). Using the LRFD load combinations in the Handbook, the governing factored axial load (kips) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: 1.4D alone; it governs only when dead load dominates.
Stops at 1.2D + 1.6L + 0.5Lr without checking the wind combinations.
Correct: 1.2D + 1.0W + L + 0.5Lr = 48 + 30 + 25 + 5 = 108 kips, the largest of the combinations.
Applies the old 1.6 factor to wind (1.2D + 1.6W + L + 0.5Lr); the current combinations use 1.0W.
A.eli5: You have to try every recipe in the load-combination list and keep the biggest result. Here the "wind" recipe wins: full wind plus full floor live load beats the recipe that pumps up only the floor live load, because the wind load is large.
A.hint: Evaluate all the LRFD combinations; do not stop at 1.2D + 1.6L.

steps.text: Combination 1.
Combination 2 (floor live load leads).
Combination 3 (roof live leads; the larger of L and 0.5W is L = 25).
Combination 4 (wind leads).
Combination 6 (wind with minimum dead load) gives 0.9(40) + 30 = 66 kips. The governing value is the largest.

traps: Assuming 1.2D + 1.6L always governs.
Using 1.6W from older editions of ASCE 7.
Dropping the companion live load L in the wind combination.

A.topic: Design of steel components (members and connections)
A.statement: A W18x50 floor beam ($F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$) spans 24 ft, simply supported under uniform load. Its compression flange is braced laterally only at the supports and at midspan, as shown, and $C_b = 1.30$ for each unbraced segment. Using the Handbook beam selection table, the LRFD design flexural strength $\phi_b M_n$ (kip-ft) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: This is $\phi_b M_r$, the strength at $L_r$; the unbraced length of 12 ft is well short of $L_r$ = 17.0 ft.
The inelastic lateral-torsional buckling value with $C_b$ = 1.0; it ignores the given $C_b$ = 1.30.
Correct: $1.30[379 - 13.1(12 - 5.83)] = 388$ kip-ft, but $\phi_b M_n$ can never exceed $\phi_b M_p$ = 379 kip-ft.
Applies $C_b$ but forgets the cap at $\phi_b M_p$.
A.eli5: A beam braced only every 12 ft can twist sideways before it reaches its full strength, so the table formula knocks some strength off. But a moment that varies along the segment (C_b above 1) gives some of it back. Here it gives back so much that the result would exceed the beam's full plastic strength, and the beam can never be stronger than that ceiling.
A.hint: Compare $L_b$ = 12 ft with $L_p$ and $L_r$ from the W18x50 row, apply $C_b$, then check the $\phi_b M_p$ ceiling.

steps.text: Read the W18x50 row of the Zx table.
steps.latex: \phi_b M_p = 379,\; \phi_b M_r = 233 \text{ kip-ft},\; BF = 13.1 \text{ kips},\; L_p = 5.83,\; L_r = 17.0 \text{ ft}

steps.text: Unbraced length is the distance between brace points; it falls in the inelastic range.
Inelastic lateral-torsional buckling strength with the given $C_b$.
Apply the ceiling.

A.handbookFormula: \phi M_n = C_b[\phi M_p - BF(L_b - L_p)] \le \phi M_p
traps: Forgetting that $C_b$ can push the result above $\phi_b M_p$, which is not allowed.
Using the full span as $L_b$ instead of the distance between braces.
Ignoring $C_b$ (taking 1.0) when it is given.

A.topic: Design of steel components (members and connections)
A.statement: A diagonal brace is a single L4x4x1/2 angle (A36: $F_y = 36 \text{ ksi}$, $F_u = 58 \text{ ksi}$, $A_g = 3.75 \text{ in}^2$) connected through one leg by three 3/4-in. bolts in standard holes in one line, as shown. Considering tensile yielding and tensile rupture only, the LRFD design tensile strength $\phi P_n$ (kips) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Correct: $A_n$ = 3.75 - 0.875(0.5) = 3.31 in², U = 1 - 1.18/6 = 0.803, $A_e$ = 2.66 in², rupture 0.75(58)(2.66) = 116 kips governs over yielding (122 kips).
Tensile yielding, 0.90(36)(3.75); it does not govern because rupture is smaller.
Rupture on the net area with U = 1.0, ignoring shear lag in an angle connected through one leg.
Rupture on the gross area: no hole deduction and no shear lag.
A.eli5: There are two ways the brace can fail in tension: the whole bar stretches too much (yielding), or it tears through the bolt holes (rupture). For rupture, take away the hole, then take away a bit more because only one leg is bolted and the force cannot spread evenly into the other leg. The smaller of the two strengths is the answer.
A.hint: Net area uses a hole of bolt diameter + 1/8 in.; U = 1 - x̄/L with L measured between the end bolts.

steps.text: Yielding on the gross area.
Net area: hole size for net area is $d_b + 1/8$ in. = 0.875 in.
Shear lag: connection length is 2 x 3 in. = 6 in. between the end bolts; x̄ = 1.18 in. from the figure.
Rupture on the effective net area.
The smaller value governs.

A.handbookFormula: \phi P_n = 0.75 F_u A_e,\; A_e = U A_n,\; U = 1 - \bar{x}/L
traps: Skipping shear lag for an angle bolted through one leg.
Using the bolt diameter, or bolt + 1/16 in., as the hole width for net area.
Measuring the connection length as 3 bolts x 3 in. instead of between the end bolts.

A.topic: Design of steel components (members and connections)
A.statement: A W14x61 column ($F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$) in a braced frame is 20 ft tall, rigidly fixed to its footing and pinned at the top, with no intermediate bracing in either axis. Using the AISC-recommended design value of K and the Handbook column table, the LRFD available axial strength $\phi_c P_n$ (kips) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Reads the table at KL = 20 ft (K = 1.0), ignoring the fixed base.
Correct: fixed-pinned, recommended K = 0.80, KL = 16 ft, and the W14x61 column of the table gives 515 kips.
Uses the theoretical K = 0.7 (KL = 14 ft); the question asks for the recommended design value.
Reads the KL = 0 row (the squash load), which ignores buckling.
A.eli5: A fixed base helps the column resist buckling, as if it were shorter. The design charts say to treat a fixed-pinned column as 0.8 times its real height, so 16 ft. Look up 16 ft in the W14x61 column of the table.
A.hint: Fixed-pinned: AISC-recommended K = 0.80. The table is entered with KL about the weak axis.

steps.text: Effective length factor for rotation fixed and translation fixed at one end, rotation free and translation fixed at the other (case b).
Effective length (same both axes; the table uses $r_y$, which governs).
Read Table 4-1, W14x61 column, KL = 16 ft.

A.handbookFormula: \phi_c P_n \text{ from AISC Table 4-1 at } KL
traps: Using the actual height instead of KL.
Taking the theoretical K (0.7) when the design value (0.80) is asked for.
Reading the wrong shape column in the table.

A.statement: At nominal flexural strength, a reinforced concrete beam with stirrups has its neutral axis 8.4 in. below the compression face. The extreme tension bars are 19.0 in. below the compression face and the centroid of all the tension steel is 17.5 in. below it. The strength reduction factor $\phi$ for flexure is most nearly:
choiceNotes: The compression-controlled value; the strain here (0.0038) is above 0.002, so the section is in the transition zone.
Computes the strain at the steel centroid (d = 17.5 in.) instead of at the extreme layer $d_t$.
Assumes the section is tension-controlled without checking; that needs $\varepsilon_t \ge 0.005$.
A.eli5: The factor depends on how much the farthest bars stretch when the concrete crushes. Draw a straight strain line from 0.003 at the top through zero at the neutral axis and read it at the bottom bars: about 0.0038. That is between 0.002 and 0.005, so the factor is in between too.
A.hint: Use $d_t$ (the extreme layer), not d, in the strain formula.

steps.text: Net tensile strain at the extreme tension layer, from similar triangles.
Classify: $0.002 < \varepsilon_t < 0.005$, a transition section.
Transition-zone factor for members with ties (stirrups).

traps: Using d instead of $d_t$.
Assuming $\phi$ = 0.90 for every beam.
Treating anything that is not tension-controlled as compression-controlled.

A.statement: Near the support of a heavily loaded transfer girder, $V_u = 100 \text{ kips}$. The web is $b_w = 14 \text{ in.}$ wide with $d = 22 \text{ in.}$, in normal-weight concrete with $f'_c = 4{,}000 \text{ psi}$. The largest stirrup spacing ACI 318 allows there (in.) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Correct: $V_c$ = 39.0 kips, $V_s$ = 100/0.75 - 39.0 = 94.4 kips, which exceeds $4b_wd\sqrt{f'_c}$ = 77.9 kips, so the limit is the smaller of d/4 = 5.5 in. and 12 in.
Uses d/2, the limit for $V_s \le 4b_wd\sqrt{f'_c}$. Getting $V_s$ as $V_u - \phi V_c$ = 70.8 kips (no division by $\phi$) leads here.
Picks the 12-in. cap from the right row but takes the larger of the two values instead of the smaller.
The 24-in. cap from the lighter-shear row, taken as the limit instead of the smaller value; it only governs beams with d over 48 in.
A.eli5: When the stirrups have to carry a lot of shear, the code wants them closer together so every possible diagonal crack crosses at least a couple of them. First work out how much shear the stirrups must take; it is more than the "heavy" threshold here, so the spacing limit drops from d/2 to d/4.
A.hint: Find $V_s = V_u/\phi - V_c$ and compare it with $4b_wd\sqrt{f'_c}$ to pick the row of the spacing table.

steps.text: Concrete shear strength.
Shear the stirrups must provide.
Threshold that sets the spacing row (and the upper limit $8b_wd\sqrt{f'_c}$ = 155.8 kips is not exceeded).
Maximum spacing for $V_s > 4b_wd\sqrt{f'_c}$: the smaller of d/4 and 12 in.

traps: Computing $V_s$ as $V_u - \phi V_c$, which understates it and picks the wrong row.
Taking the larger of the two limits instead of the smaller.
Forgetting to convert $V_c$ from pounds to kips.

A.statement: The singly reinforced beam section shown has five #9 bars in two rows ($f'_c = 4{,}000 \text{ psi}$, $f_y = 60 \text{ ksi}$, stirrups). The design flexural strength $\phi M_n$ (kip-ft) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Uses the upper row depth (20.5 in.) as d instead of the centroid of all five bars.
Correct: d = 22.3 in. to the bar centroid, a = 6.30 in., $\varepsilon_t$ = 0.0065 so $\phi$ = 0.90, and $\phi M_n$ = 0.90(300)(22.3 - 3.15)/12 = 431 kip-ft.
Uses the lower row depth (23.5 in.) as d; that is $d_t$, which belongs in the strain check, not in the moment arm.
This is $M_n$; it leaves out $\phi$ = 0.90.
A.eli5: The steel pulls with its full yield force, and the concrete pushes back over a block at the top. The lever arm runs from the middle of that block down to the middle of all the steel, which sits between the two rows, closer to the bottom row because it has more bars. The bottom bars stretch plenty, so the full 0.90 factor applies.
A.hint: Take d to the centroid of the five bars; use $d_t$ (the lower row) only for the strain check.

steps.text: Steel area and effective depth to the centroid of the bars (3 bars at 23.5 in., 2 at 20.5 in.).
Depth of the stress block.
Strain check at the extreme layer: c = a/0.85 = 7.41 in.
Nominal and design moment.
Apply the factor.

A.handbookFormula: M_n = A_s f_y\left(d - \dfrac{a}{2}\right),\; a = \dfrac{A_s f_y}{0.85 f'_c b}
traps: Using the lower row depth as d.
Using the overall height h as d.
Forgetting $\phi$, or assuming it without the strain check.

B.topic: Analysis of statically determinate trusses, beams and frames
B.statement: The pedestrian bridge shown is a Pratt truss with inclined end posts. The deck hangs from the bottom chord and puts 15 kips on each of joints L1 through L5. The truss has a pin at L0 and a roller at L6. The force in top chord member U2U3 (kips) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Takes moments about U2 instead of L3: 37.5(24) - 15(12) = 720 kip-ft, and 720 / 9 = 80 kips is the force in bottom chord L2L3, not in the top chord.

Correct: cut through U2U3, U2L3 and L2L3 and take moments about L3, where the other two cut members meet: 37.5(36) - 15(24) - 15(12) = 810 kip-ft, and 810 / 9 = 90 kips, pushing on the joint (compression).
Right size, wrong sense. Under gravity load a simply supported truss sags, so its top chord is squeezed, not stretched.
Leaves out the 15-kip load at L2 when summing moments about L3: (1,350 - 360) / 9 = 110 kips.
B.eli5: Cut the bridge with a vertical saw just right of U2 and look at the left piece. The support pushes up 37.5 kips, two deck loads push down, and together they try to rotate the piece about joint L3. The top chord is the only cut member that can stop that rotation, because the other two pass right through L3. It sits 9 ft above L3, so it must push with 810 / 9 = 90 kips.
B.hint: Choose the moment point where two of the three cut members meet, so only U2U3 is left in the equation.

steps.text: Reactions: five 15-kip loads, placed symmetrically, so each support takes half.
Cut through panel 3: members U2U3, U2L3 (the diagonal) and L2L3. The diagonal and the bottom chord both pass through L3, so take moments about L3 (x = 36 ft) on the left piece.
Solve for the force in the top chord, with F taken as a push on the cut (compression).
Sense: the moment from the left piece about L3 is sagging, so the top fibre of the truss, the top chord, is in compression.

B.handbookFormula: \Sigma M = 0 \text{ on a section free body (method of sections)}
traps: Taking moments about U2, which gives the bottom chord L2L3 instead.
Forgetting a load that sits on the free body (the load at L2 is left of the cut).
Calling the top chord of a sagging truss a tension member.

B.topic: Analysis of statically determinate trusses, beams and frames
B.statement: The equipment-platform frame shown has a pin at A, a roller at D and rigid knees at B and C. It carries a uniform load of 1.5 kips/ft on girder BC and a horizontal load of 6 kips at B. The bending moment at the top of column AB, at knee B (kip-ft), is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Assumes a column on a pin carries no moment. The pin has no moment at A itself, but it takes a horizontal reaction, and that force bends the column all the way up to B.
Splits the 6-kip horizontal load equally between the two bases. A roller cannot take a horizontal force, so the pin at A takes all 6 kips.
This is wL^2/8 = 1.5(16)^2/8, the midspan moment of a simply supported 16-ft girder, not the moment at the knee.
Correct: the pin at A takes the whole 6-kip horizontal reaction, and it acts 12 ft below B, so M_B = 6(12) = 72 kip-ft.
B.eli5: The roller at D can only push up, so the pin at A has to supply the whole sideways push of 6 kips. That sideways force at the foot of a 12-ft column bends it like a lever: 6 kips times 12 ft is 72 kip-ft at the top. The girder load does not change this, because it only adds vertical forces, and vertical forces at A pass straight up the column.
B.hint: Find the horizontal reaction at A first; then take a free body of column AB alone.

steps.text: Horizontal equilibrium: the roller at D has no horizontal reaction, so A takes it all.
Vertical reactions from moments about A (for completeness).
Free body of column AB: A_y runs along the column axis and makes no moment; H_A acts 12 ft below B.
Check from the girder side: column CD has only a vertical reaction, so its moment at C is zero, and the girder moment at B is D_y(16) minus the girder load moment.

traps: Sharing the horizontal reaction between a pin and a roller.
Thinking a pinned base means the whole column is moment-free.
Reporting the girder midspan moment instead of the knee moment.

B.topic: Analysis of statically determinate trusses, beams and frames
B.statement: A loading-dock beam rests on a pin at A and a roller at B and overhangs 6 ft past B to a free end C, as shown. It carries a uniform load of 2 kips/ft over its full 26-ft length. The maximum positive bending moment in span AB (kip-ft) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: This is the negative moment over support B from the overhang, w(6)^2/2 = 36 kip-ft, not the largest positive moment.
Subtracts the whole support moment from wL^2/8 (100 - 36). The support moment at B fades to zero at A, so at midspan only half of it acts.
Correct: R_A = 18.2 kips, shear is zero 9.1 ft from A, and M = 18.2^2 / (2 x 2) = 82.8 kip-ft.
wL^2/8 for a 20-ft simple span, ignoring the overhang load that lifts A and lowers the span moment.
B.eli5: The load hanging on the overhang acts like a child on the short end of a see-saw: it pulls the beam down past B and lifts a little of the load off A. So A carries less than half of the span load, the beam sags a bit less, and the peak of the sag moves a little left of center. The peak is where the shear crosses zero.
B.hint: Find R_A from moments about B, then find where the shear is zero.

steps.text: Reaction at B from moments about A. The total load 2(26) = 52 kips acts at 13 ft.
Reaction at A.
Shear in span AB is V = R_A - wx; it is zero where the moment peaks.
Moment at that point.

traps: Using wL^2/8 for the span and forgetting the overhang.
Taking the maximum at midspan instead of where the shear is zero.
Reporting the support (negative) moment when the positive one is asked.

B.topic: Deflection of statically determinate beams, trusses and frames
B.statement: The wall bracket shown supports a 20-kip hoist load hanging from joint C. Tie AC and strut BC are steel ($E = 29{,}000 \text{ ksi}$) with the cross-sectional areas marked on the figure. Using the unit load method, the vertical deflection of joint C (in.) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Right sum, but the member lengths were entered in feet while E is in ksi and A in in.^2, so the answer is 12 times too small.
Counts only the tie AC. The strut shortens, and a shortening strut lets C drop just as much as a stretching tie does: its term is positive too.
Adds up FL/AE for each member without multiplying by the unit-load force f. Both f values exceed 1 here, so this is too small.
Correct: the sum of fFL/AE is 0.0883 (tie) + 0.0862 (strut) = 0.175 in. downward.
B.eli5: Load the bracket and each bar changes length a little: the tie stretches and the strut shortens. The unit load method asks how much each bar's change in length moves C downward. That "lever" for each bar is its force under a 1-kip load at C. Multiply each bar's change in length by its lever, add them up, and you have the drop at C.
B.hint: Get the member forces for the 20-kip load and for a 1-kip load at C; then sum fFL/(AE) with L in inches.

steps.text: Geometry: strut BC runs 12 ft across and 9 ft up, so it is 15 ft long.
Joint C under the 20-kip load: only the strut has a vertical component.
Unit load at C (1 kip down): the forces scale by 1/20.
Tie AC: L = 144 in., A = 2.0 in.^2.
Strut BC: L = 180 in., A = 4.0 in.^2. Both forces are compression, so the product is positive.
Add. A positive result means C moves in the direction of the unit load (down).

traps: Leaving the member lengths in feet.
Dropping the compression member, or giving its term a negative sign when both F and f are compressive.
Forgetting the unit-load force f in each term.

B.topic: Deflection of statically determinate beams, trusses and frames
B.statement: A simply supported steel beam ($E = 29{,}000 \text{ ksi}$) spans 30 ft and carries a 20-kip live load at midspan from a hanging mechanical unit. To keep the live-load deflection within L/360, the minimum moment of inertia of the beam (in.^4) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Uses PL^3/(192EI), the case for a beam fixed at both ends. This beam is simply supported.
Spreads the 20 kips over the span and uses 5wL^4/(384EI). A point load at midspan bends the beam more than the same load spread out.
Correct: the limit is 360/360 = 1.00 in., and I = PL^3/(48E x 1.00) = 670 in.^4.
Uses PL^3/(3EI), the cantilever case, which is 16 times the simple-span deflection.
B.eli5: L/360 means the beam may sag one 360th of its length: 30 ft is 360 in., so 1 in. The Handbook gives the sag of a simple beam with a load in the middle, PL^3/(48EI). Set that equal to 1 in. and solve for the stiffness I the beam needs.
B.hint: Work in kips and inches throughout: L = 360 in.

steps.text: Allowable deflection.
Midspan deflection of a simple beam with a central point load (Handbook beam table).
Set the deflection equal to the limit and solve for I.

traps: Mixing feet and inches: L must be 360 in. in both the formula and the limit.
Picking the wrong beam-table case (uniform load, cantilever, or fixed ends).

B.statement: A highway sign pole is a round steel tube ($E = 29{,}000 \text{ ksi}$) with a 6.0-in. outside diameter and a 0.25-in. wall. It is 18 ft tall, fixed at its base and free at its top, as shown. Using the theoretical effective-length factor, the Euler buckling load (kips) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Uses K = 2.1, the recommended design value for a flagpole column. The statement asks for the theoretical value, K = 2.0.
Uses K = 2.0 but does not square it: pi^2 EI / (K L^2). The whole effective length KL is squared.
Uses K = 1.0, as if the top were pinned. A free top lets the pole sway, which doubles the effective length.
B.eli5: A pole fixed at the ground and free at the top bends like half of a pinned column twice as tall. So its effective length is twice its real height, 36 ft. Because buckling load drops with the square of length, doubling the length cuts the load to one quarter.
B.hint: Fixed-free: K = 2.0. Compute I of the hollow circle from the outside and inside diameters.

steps.text: Inside diameter and moment of inertia of the tube.
Effective length with the theoretical fixed-free factor.
Euler load.

traps: Using K = 1.0 for a free top.
Squaring L but not K.
Using the recommended design K when the theoretical one is asked.

B.topic: Determinacy and stability of beams, trusses and frames
B.statement: The truss shown has a pin at L0 and a roller at L3. Its first panel has two crossing diagonals, its middle panel has none, and its last panel has one. The truss is best classified as:

choices.text: Stable and indeterminate to the first degree
Stable and indeterminate to the second degree

choiceNotes: Correct: the middle panel is a rectangle of four pinned bars with no diagonal, so it can rack into a parallelogram. The extra diagonal in the first panel does not help; it only makes that panel redundant.
This is what the count alone says (m + r = 13 + 3 = 16 = 2j). The count is necessary but not sufficient; the bars must also be arranged to make triangles.
Counts the roller as a pin (r = 4), so m + r - 2j = 1, and misses that the middle panel has nothing to stop it from racking.
Counts the roller as a pin (r = 4) and then adds the visibly extra diagonal in the first panel as one more redundant on top of the count, so that bar is counted twice. The middle panel still racks.
B.eli5: A truss is stiff because triangles cannot change shape. The middle panel is a rectangle, and a rectangle of pinned bars folds into a parallelogram with a push. Putting a second diagonal in the first panel makes the bar count come out right, but that extra bar is in the wrong place: it stiffens a panel that was already stiff and does nothing for the floppy one.
B.hint: Do the count, then look at each panel: is every panel made of triangles?

steps.text: Count: 3 bottom chords, 3 top chords, 4 verticals and 3 diagonals; 8 joints; pin plus roller gives 3 reactions.
Classification by count.
Check the arrangement. The middle panel U1-U2-L2-L1 is a four-bar rectangle: it can rack (shear) with no change in bar length, so the truss is a mechanism.

The count balanced only because the first panel has one redundant diagonal; one redundant plus one mechanism still adds up to 2j. The Handbook notes that stability also requires an appropriate arrangement of members.

traps: Trusting m + r = 2j without looking at the arrangement of the bars.
Thinking a redundant bar in one panel can make up for a missing bar in another.

B.statement: A balcony beam is built into a concrete core wall at A and propped by a column at B, as shown, and carries a 24-kip load at midspan. EI is constant. The vertical reaction at B (kips) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: This is 3P/16, the coefficient of the fixed-end moment (3PL/16) used as if it were the reaction.
Correct: the wall moment is 3PL/16 = 90 kip-ft, and moments about A give R_B = (240 - 90)/20 = 7.5 kips (= 5P/16).
P/2, the reaction of a simply supported beam. The fixed end at A takes more than half of the load.
This is the reaction at the wall A (11P/16), not at the prop.
B.eli5: If the beam were only resting on two supports, each would carry half the load, 12 kips. But end A is built into the wall, which stiffens that end and pulls more of the load toward it. The Handbook gives the wall moment for this case, and with that one number the rest is just a see-saw balance about A.
B.hint: The Handbook fixed-end moment table has a case with one end fixed and the other pinned.

steps.text: Fixed-end moment at A for a propped cantilever with a midspan load (Handbook table).
Moments about A on the whole beam. The wall moment resists the clockwise turning of the load.
Solve.
Check by compatibility: the cantilever tip deflection from P equals the tip deflection the prop removes.

B.handbookFormula: (FEM)_{AB} = \dfrac{3PL}{16} \text{ (fixed at A, pinned at B, load at midspan)}
traps: Treating the beam as simply supported.
Reporting the wall reaction instead of the prop reaction.
Getting the direction of the wall moment wrong in the moment sum.

B.statement: A parking-garage beam is built in at both ends and spans 30 ft with a uniform load of 2.4 kips/ft, as shown. EI is constant. The distance from support A to the nearest inflection point (ft) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Uses wL^2/24 as the end moment. That is the positive moment at midspan; the end moment is twice as large, wL^2/12.
Correct: with M_A = -wL^2/12 = -180 kip-ft and V_A = 36 kips, M(x) = 36x - 1.2x^2 - 180 = 0 at x = 6.34 ft (0.211L).
L/4: the inflection point of a propped cantilever under uniform load, measured from its fixed end. With both ends fixed it moves closer to the supports.
Uses wL^2/8 as the end moment; the moment then only just touches zero at midspan, which is not an inflection point of this beam.
B.eli5: A beam held tight at both ends curls upward near the walls (hogging) and sags in the middle. Somewhere between, the bending changes direction: that is the inflection point, where the moment is zero. Write the moment along the beam using the end moment wL^2/12 from the Handbook and find where it crosses zero.
B.hint: By symmetry each end shear is wL/2. Use the fixed-end moment wL^2/12 as a negative moment at A.

steps.text: End moment and end shear by symmetry.
Moment at distance x from A.
Set M(x) = 0.
Take the root nearest A.

traps: Using the midspan moment wL^2/24 or the simple-span wL^2/8 as the end moment.
Carrying over the L/4 rule from a propped cantilever.

B.topic: Loads, load combinations and load paths
B.statement: The beam shown has a pin at A, a roller at B and an 8-ft overhang to C. It carries a dead load of 1.0 kip/ft over its full length and a uniform live load of 2.0 kips/ft that may occupy any part or parts of the beam. Using the influence line for the reaction at A, the maximum service (D + L) reaction at A (kips) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Places the live load correctly (on AB only) but leaves out the dead load, which is always present.
Puts the live load on the whole beam. Live load on the overhang lifts A, so it lowers the reaction there.
Correct: dead load on everything gives 1.0(12 - 1.33) = 10.7 kips; live load on AB only gives 2.0(12) = 24 kips; the total is 34.7 kips.
Ignores the overhang and treats AB as a 24-ft simple span with 3.0 kips/ft: 3.0(24)/2 = 36 kips.
B.eli5: The influence line tells you how much of a 1-kip load placed anywhere reaches support A. Between A and B the answer is positive (load there pushes down on A). On the overhang it is negative (load there tips the beam over B and lifts A). Dead load is everywhere whether you like it or not, but live load can be placed where it hurts most: only where the line is positive.
B.hint: Draw the influence line for R_A: 1 at A, 0 at B, and a negative value at C. Load the live load only on the positive part.

steps.text: Influence line for R_A: a straight line from 1.0 at A to 0 at B, continuing to a negative ordinate at C.
Areas under the influence line.
Dead load acts over the full length, so it uses the net area.
Live load placed on the positive region only (span AB).
Maximum service reaction.

B.handbookFormula: \text{Effect} = w \times (\text{area under the influence line over the loaded length})
traps: Loading the live load over the whole beam, including the part where the influence line is negative.
Skipping the dead load, or placing the dead load only where it helps.
Ignoring the overhang.

B.topic: Loads, load combinations and load paths
B.statement: In the framing plan shown, the floor slab spans between the beams, and each beam is simply supported on the girders. The dead load is 70 psf (slab and framing) and the live load is 100 psf. Ignoring live load reduction and using the governing LRFD load combination, the factored maximum moment in interior beam B1 (kip-ft) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Uses 1.4D, which ignores the live load. With this much live load, 1.2D + 1.6L governs.
Uses a 4-ft tributary width (half the spacing on one side only). An interior beam collects half a bay from each side: 8 ft in all.
Unfactored load, (70 + 100)(8) = 1.36 kips/ft, gives the service moment, not the factored one.
B.eli5: Each beam holds up the strip of floor that is closer to it than to its neighbours: half the gap on its left plus half on its right, 8 ft wide. Multiply the floor loads, with their safety factors, by that strip width to get load per foot along the beam, then use the simple-beam moment wL^2/8.
B.hint: Tributary width of an interior beam = half the spacing on each side.

steps.text: Tributary width of B1: half of 8 ft on each side.
Governing combination: 1.4D = 98 psf is far less than 1.2D + 1.6L.
Line load on the beam.
Maximum moment of the simply supported 24-ft beam.

traps: Using the beam spacing on one side only for the tributary width.
Using service loads where factored loads are asked.
Stopping at 1.4D.

B.topic: Design of steel components (members and connections)
B.statement: A floor beam of $F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$ steel has its top flange welded to the metal deck, so it is fully braced and lateral-torsional buckling does not govern. The factored moment is $M_u = 380 \text{ kip-ft}$. Using the Handbook's W-shape selection table by $Z_x$, the lightest adequate W-shape is:
choiceNotes: Correct: the W21x48 has a design strength of 398 kip-ft, more than 380, and no lighter shape in the table reaches 380.
Drops the resistance factor (Z_x >= 380(12)/50 = 91.2 in.^3) and takes the first row that meets it reading up the table, W16x50 (Z_x = 92.0 in.^3). Its design strength is only 345 kip-ft.
Its design strength, 379 kip-ft, is the closest value in the table but is just below 380, so it is not adequate.
Adequate (383 kip-ft) and the first shape above 380 when reading up the table, but at 61 lb/ft it is heavier than the W21x48.
B.eli5: The table lists beams in order of strength, not weight. The first beam strong enough is not always the lightest one: deeper beams get their strength from depth instead of steel, so a deeper, lighter beam a few rows further up can do the job for less weight. Check every strong-enough shape near the top of the list and pick the lightest.
B.hint: Read the design-strength column (phi_b M_px), keep every shape with at least 380 kip-ft, then compare weights.

steps.text: Requirement: the design flexural strength, read from the table's phi_b M_px column, is at least the factored moment (fully braced, so L_b is not a concern).
Shapes near the cut-off in the table: W18x50 = 379 (fails), W14x61 = 383, W16x57 = 394, W21x48 = 398 (all pass).
Lighter shapes all fall short: W21x44 = 358, W18x46 = 340, W16x45 = 309 kip-ft. The lightest passing shape is the W21x48.

traps: Taking the first adequate row instead of the lightest adequate shape.
Forgetting the resistance factor and choosing from Z_x alone.
Accepting a shape that is a hair under the demand.

B.topic: Design of steel components (members and connections)
B.statement: A W12x58 column ($F_y = 50 \text{ ksi}$, $A = 17.0 \text{ in}^2$, $r_x = 5.28 \text{ in.}$, $r_y = 2.51 \text{ in.}$) in a warehouse wall is 30 ft tall and pinned at both ends. Wall girts brace its weak axis at the third points; the strong axis has no intermediate bracing, as shown. Using the AISC column equations, the design compressive strength $\phi_c P_n$ (kips) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Ignores the girts and uses KL/r_y = 360/2.51 = 143. The weak axis is braced every 10 ft.
Right slenderness and F_cr, but no resistance factor: this is P_n, not phi P_n.
Assumes the weak axis always governs and uses KL/r_y = 47.8. With the girts at third points, the strong axis is now the more slender one.
B.eli5: A column buckles in whichever direction it is floppiest. The girts hold the weak direction every 10 ft, so in that direction it is a stubby 10-ft column. In the strong direction nothing holds it for the full 30 ft. Compare length divided by stiffness (KL/r) in both directions; the bigger number is the one that buckles first, and it sets the strength.
B.hint: Compute KL/r for each axis with its own unbraced length; the larger one governs.

steps.text: Slenderness about each axis (K = 1.0).
The strong axis governs. Check the range: 68.2 is below 4.71 sqrt(E/F_y), so the inelastic equation applies.
Elastic buckling stress.
Critical stress.
Design strength.

traps: Assuming the weak axis always controls.
Ignoring intermediate bracing.
Leaving out phi_c = 0.90.

B.topic: Design of steel components (members and connections)
B.statement: A flat-bar brace, PL 1/2 x 6 of A36 steel ($F_y = 36 \text{ ksi}$, $F_u = 58 \text{ ksi}$), is bolted to a gusset with six 3/4-in. bolts in two lines, as shown. Using the Handbook's hole allowance for net area, the block shear design strength of the bar end (kips) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Correct: the yield-on-shear form, 0.6F_y A_gv + F_u A_nt = 223.6 kips, is smaller than the rupture form (246.5 kips), so R_n = 223.6 and phi R_n = 0.75(223.6) = 168 kips.
Uses the rupture form 0.6F_u A_nv + F_u A_nt = 246.5 kips without checking the cap 0.6F_y A_gv + F_u A_nt, which is smaller here.
Correct nominal strength, but the resistance factor phi = 0.75 is left out.
Uses gross areas on every plane, deducting no holes: 0.75[0.6(58)(7.5) + 58(1.5)].
B.eli5: Block shear is the bolts tearing a chunk out of the end of the bar: the chunk slides out along the two bolt lines (shear) and rips across between them (tension). The Handbook adds up the strength of those tear lines, but caps the shear part at the yield strength of the full, unholed shear planes. Take the smaller of the two expressions, then apply phi = 0.75.
B.hint: Shear planes run along each bolt line from the bar end to the last bolt; the tension plane runs between the two lines. Hole width for net area = bolt diameter + 1/8 in.

steps.text: Gross shear area: two planes, each 1.5 + 3 + 3 = 7.5 in. long.
Net shear area: each plane passes through 2.5 holes; the Handbook hole allowance is d_b + 1/8 = 0.875 in.
Net tension area between the bolt lines (one hole width out of the 3-in. gage).
Both forms of the block shear equation (U_bs = 1.0).
Take the smaller and apply phi.

traps: Skipping the upper limit on the shear term.
Using the bolt diameter instead of bolt diameter + 1/8 in. for the hole deduction.
Counting 3 holes per shear line instead of 2.5 (the last hole is cut in half by the block edge).

B.statement: A beam is to carry four #9 bottom bars in one layer inside #3 stirrups, with 1.5 in. clear cover to the stirrups and concrete with a 1-in. maximum aggregate size, as shown. The clear space between bars must be at least the largest of 1 in., the bar diameter, and 4/3 of the maximum aggregate size. Neglecting the stirrup bend radius, the minimum beam width b (in.) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Uses a 1-in. clear space; the aggregate rule (4/3 x 1 in. = 1.33 in.) governs here.
Uses the bar diameter, 1.128 in., as the clear space; the aggregate rule gives more.
Counts four clear spaces for four bars. There are only three spaces between four bars.
B.eli5: Add up everything that sits side by side across the bottom of the beam: the cover on each side, the stirrup leg on each side, the four bars, and the three gaps between them. The gap must be wide enough for the largest stones in the concrete to flow through, which here means 1.33 in.
B.hint: Width = 2 covers + 2 stirrup diameters + n bar diameters + (n - 1) clear spaces.

steps.text: Bar diameters from the Handbook bar table.
Minimum clear space: the largest of the three limits.
Add the parts across the width.

traps: Counting n spaces instead of n - 1.
Forgetting the stirrup legs.
Not checking all three spacing limits.

B.statement: A one-way floor slab is 7 in. thick with #5 bottom bars at 10 in. on center and 0.75 in. clear cover, as shown ($f'_c = 4{,}000 \text{ psi}$, $f_y = 60{,}000 \text{ psi}$). The design moment strength $\phi M_n$ per foot of slab width (kip-ft/ft) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Uses one bar (0.31 in.^2) per foot. Bars at 10 in. put 12/10 of a bar in each foot: 0.372 in.^2/ft.
Correct: A_s = 0.372 in.^2/ft, d = 5.94 in., a = 0.547 in., the section is tension-controlled, and phi M_n = 0.9(126.4)/12 = 9.48 kip-ft/ft.
This is M_n (10.5 kip-ft/ft) with no resistance factor.
Uses the full thickness, 7 in., as d. The effective depth runs only to the center of the bars.
B.eli5: Treat the slab as a beam 12 in. wide. Count how much steel falls in that 12-in. strip (1.2 bars), find how deep the bars sit (thickness minus cover minus half a bar), then use the usual beam formula. A thin slab with light steel is always tension-controlled, so phi is 0.9.
B.hint: A_s per foot = bar area x 12 / spacing. d = h - cover - d_b/2.

steps.text: Steel area in a 12-in. strip.
Effective depth.
Depth of the stress block.
Check strain: c = a/0.85 = 0.644 in.
Nominal and design strength.

B.handbookFormula: M_n = A_s f_y\left(d - \dfrac{a}{2}\right),\; a = \dfrac{A_s f_y}{0.85 f'_c b}
traps: Using one bar per foot instead of converting the spacing.
Taking d as the slab thickness.
Leaving the answer in kip-in. or leaving out phi.

B.statement: A rectangular beam is 12 in. wide with one layer of tension bars at $d = d_t = 20 \text{ in.}$ ($f'_c = 4{,}000 \text{ psi}$, $f_y = 60 \text{ ksi}$, no compression steel). The largest area of tension steel (in^2) for which the section is still tension-controlled is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Correct: tension-controlled means c is at most 0.375d_t = 7.5 in.; a = 0.85(7.5) = 6.375 in., and A_s = 0.85(4)(6.375)(12)/60 = 4.34 in.^2.
Uses a net tensile strain of 0.004 (c = 3d/7), the older minimum for beams. That section is in the transition zone, not tension-controlled.
Sets a = c = 7.5 in., forgetting that the stress block depth is beta_1 times c.
The balanced condition (c = 0.6d_t, strain 0.002): that is the compression-controlled limit, far past tension-controlled.
B.eli5: Adding steel makes the concrete squeeze zone deeper, and a deeper squeeze zone means the steel stretches less before the concrete crushes. To count as tension-controlled, the steel has to stretch at least 0.005, which caps the squeeze zone at 3/8 of the depth. Find the steel that makes exactly that squeeze zone.
B.hint: From the strain diagram, epsilon_t = 0.005 gives c = 0.375 d_t. Then a = beta_1 c and A_s f_y = 0.85 f'_c a b.

steps.text: Tension-controlled limit from the strain diagram.
Stress block depth with beta_1 = 0.85 for 4,000 psi concrete.
Force balance: steel tension equals concrete compression.

traps: Using c = 0.6d (the balanced or compression-controlled limit).
Forgetting beta_1 between c and a.
Using the old 0.004 strain limit.

A.statement: A sample from a levee borrow area has 38% retained on the No. 4 sieve, 54% passing the No. 4 and retained on the No. 200, and 8% passing the No. 200. Its gradation curve gives $D_{10} = 0.09$ mm, $D_{30} = 0.42$ mm and $D_{60} = 2.1$ mm, and the fines have $LL = 32$ and $PL = 19$. What is the USCS group symbol?
choiceNotes: Treats the soil as having more than 12% fines. With 8% fines (between 5 and 12%), USCS requires a dual symbol.
Correct: a sand (gravel is only 41% of the coarse fraction), poorly graded because $C_c = 0.93 < 1$, with clayey fines (PI = 13 plots above the A-line), so SP-SC.
Calls the fines silt. With $PI = 13$ and the A-line at $0.73(32 - 20) = 8.8$, the fines plot above the A-line and are clay (CL).
Checks only $C_u = 23.3 \ge 6$. Well graded also needs $1 \le C_c \le 3$, and $C_c = 0.93$ fails, so the sand is poorly graded.
A.eli5: Name the soil in three bites. First, is it mostly coarse or fine? Only 8% is fine, so it is coarse. Of the coarse part, more is sand than gravel, so it is a sand. Second, is the sand nicely spread over many sizes? It needs both a big spread (Cu) and a smooth curve (Cc between 1 and 3); Cc misses, so it is poorly graded, SP. Third, 8% fines sits in the in-between band, so you add a second symbol that says what the fines are. Their PI is above the A-line, so they act like clay: SP-SC.
A.hint: Coarse or fine first, then gravel or sand by the coarse fraction, then Cu and Cc, then the fines on the plasticity chart. 5 to 12% fines means a dual symbol.

steps.text: Only 8% passes the No. 200 sieve, so 92% is retained: more than 50%, the soil is coarse-grained.
Gravel versus sand uses the coarse fraction. Gravel (retained on No. 4) is 38 of the 92 points, under half, so the soil is a sand.
Fines of 8% fall between 5% and 12%, so the symbol is dual: gradation symbol plus fines symbol.
Gradation coefficients. A well-graded sand needs $C_u \ge 6$ and $1 \le C_c \le 3$.
Since $C_c < 1$, the sand is poorly graded: SP.
Fines: $PI = 32 - 19 = 13$. The A-line at $LL = 32$ is $0.73(32 - 20) = 8.8$. PI is above the A-line and above 7, so the fines are clay (CL).
Combine: poorly graded sand with clay.

traps: Deciding gravel versus sand from the whole sample instead of the coarse fraction (here both give sand, but not always).
Stopping at $C_u \ge 6$ and calling the sand well graded without checking $C_c$.
Giving a single symbol when fines are between 5% and 12%.
Comparing PI with 4 or 7 alone instead of with the A-line value at the given LL.

A.statement: A county road subgrade soil has 58% passing the No. 200 sieve, a liquid limit of 46 and a plasticity index of 19. What is its AASHTO classification, including the group index?
choiceNotes: A-6 requires $LL \le 40$. With $LL = 46$ the soil is in A-7.
Uses the subgroup rule backwards. A-7-5 needs $PI \le LL - 30 = 16$; here $PI = 19 > 16$, so it is A-7-6.
Right group, but stops after the first term of the group index ($23 \times 0.23 = 5.3$) and leaves out $0.01(F - 15)(PI - 10) = 3.9$.
Correct: more than 35% fines, $LL \ge 41$ and $PI \ge 11$ give A-7; $PI = 19 > LL - 30 = 16$ gives A-7-6; GI = 5.3 + 3.9 = 9.2, reported as 9.
A.eli5: AASHTO sorts soils for roads from best (A-1) to worst (A-7). With more than 35% fines this is a silty or clayey soil. Its liquid limit over 40 and PI over 10 put it in A-7, the clayey and compressible group. Because the PI is higher than LL minus 30, it is the more plastic A-7-6 branch. The group index then grades it inside the group; bigger is worse, and both parts of the formula count.
A.hint: More than 35% passing No. 200 puts it in A-4 to A-7. Use LL and PI to pick the group, LL - 30 to split A-7, then compute GI with both terms.

steps.text: Fines are 58%, more than 35%, so the soil is a silt-clay material (A-4 to A-7).
LL = 46 is 41 or more and PI = 19 is 11 or more, so the group is A-7.
Split A-7 with $LL - 30$: PI greater than that value means A-7-6.
Group index with $F = 58$:
First term and second term:
Add and round to the nearest whole number.

traps: Reading the A-7 subgroup rule backwards: A-7-6 is the one with $PI > LL - 30$.
Dropping the second term of the group index.
Putting the soil in A-6 by looking at PI only and ignoring the LL limit of 40.

A.statement: In a sand-cone test on a compacted embankment lift, the moist soil dug from the test hole weighs 6.85 lb. The sand that filled the hole (cone correction already removed) weighs 5.30 lb, and the calibrated unit weight of the sand is 96.0 pcf. The water content of the excavated soil is 11.5%. What is the dry unit weight of the fill?
choiceNotes: Divides the sand unit weight, 96.0 pcf, by $(1 + w)$. The calibration sand only measures the hole volume; its unit weight is not the soil unit weight.
Removes the water with $\gamma(1 - w)$. Water content is a fraction of the dry weight, so the correct step is $\gamma/(1 + w)$.
Correct: hole volume = 5.30/96.0 = 0.0552 ft³, moist unit weight = 124.1 pcf, dry unit weight = 124.1/1.115 = 111.3 pcf.
This is the moist (total) unit weight. The question asks for the dry unit weight, one more step.
A.eli5: The sand cone is a way to measure the size of a hole. You pour sand of known density into the hole, weigh how much went in, and that tells you the hole volume. The soil you dug out of that same hole, divided by the volume, is how heavy the fill is per cubic foot. Then take the water out by dividing by 1 plus the water content.
A.hint: The sand gives the volume of the hole. Soil weight over that volume is the moist unit weight; divide by (1 + w) for dry.

steps.text: Volume of the hole from the sand that filled it:
Moist unit weight of the fill:
Dry unit weight, with $w = 0.115$:

traps: Using $\gamma(1 - w)$ instead of $\gamma/(1 + w)$; water content is based on the dry weight.
Stopping at the moist unit weight.
Confusing the calibration sand unit weight with the soil unit weight.

A.statement: Soil stockpiled for a subgrade lift is at a water content of 9%. It is to be compacted at a water content of 14% to a dry unit weight of 112 pcf. About how many gallons of water must be added per cubic yard of compacted fill? Use 1 ft³ = 7.48 gal.

A.statement: An engineer needs the in-place undrained shear strength of a soft, sensitive clay between depths of 10 ft and 30 ft below a planned embankment. Which field test measures this most directly?

choices.text: Plate load test at the ground surface

choiceNotes: Correct: the vane is pushed into the clay at depth and rotated; the torque at failure gives the undrained shear strength directly, with little disturbance.

SPT is for granular soils, the plate load test is shallow, and the sand cone gives density, not strength. The vane is the direct choice.

A mat foundation 4 ft below grade, bearing on the clay

A.statement: A pavement subgrade is a fat clay (CH) with a plasticity index of 38. It is weak when wet and swells seasonally. Which treatment is the usual first choice to stabilize it?

choices.text: Mix in portland cement, a few percent by weight
Mix in asphalt emulsion to waterproof the clay
Compact it harder at a water content dry of optimum
Mix in lime to cut plasticity and gain strength

choiceNotes: Cement works best in granular and low-plasticity soils. A fat clay is hard to pulverize and mix with cement, and lime is the standard first step for high-PI clay.
Asphalt (bituminous) stabilization suits sands and gravels; it does not treat the plasticity of a fat clay.
Compacting a high-PI clay dry of optimum leaves it with more swell potential when it later wets up, the opposite of what is wanted.

Lime treatment is the usual first choice.

choices.text: Drainage: carrying water along the plane of the fabric
Filtration: passing water across while holding back soil
Reinforcement: adding tensile strength to carry the load
Separation: keeping the stone and the clay from mixing

choiceNotes: In-plane drainage moves water sideways inside a thick fabric or drainage composite. The problem here is intermixing, not water collecting at the interface.
Filtration matters wherever water crosses the fabric, but the failure described is the two materials mixing, which is the separation function.

steps.text: The failure described is intermixing: fines pumping up into the base and aggregate punching into the subgrade.

Keeping two different materials from mixing is the separation function of a geotextile.

traps: Choosing reinforcement for any soft subgrade even when bearing is adequate.

choices.text: Sawed transverse contraction joints: make shrinkage and temperature cracks form along chosen straight lines
Dowel bars across transverse joints: tie the slabs together so the joint cannot open

Tie bars across the longitudinal joint: carry wheel loads across while letting the slabs slide apart

choiceNotes: Correct: concrete shrinks and curls and will crack somewhere; a sawed contraction joint is a planned weak line so the crack forms there, straight and sealable.

A.statement: A long 2H:1V cut slope on a new highway has just been graded to final shape, and rain is forecast before grass can grow. Which measure prevents erosion on the slope itself, rather than catching sediment after the soil has already moved?

choices.text: A silt fence along the toe of the slope
A temporary sediment basin at the low point of the site
Inlet protection on the storm drains downstream
Seeding covered by a staked erosion control blanket

choiceNotes: A silt fence is a sediment control: it slows runoff and traps soil that has already eroded from the slope above it.
A sediment basin settles out soil that has already been carried off the slope; it does nothing to keep soil in place.
Inlet protection filters sediment out of runoff at the drain; the slope still erodes.
Correct: a blanket over seed shields the bare soil from raindrop impact and sheet flow until vegetation takes hold. That is erosion control at the source.
A.eli5: There are two jobs: keep dirt from leaving the slope, and catch the dirt that leaves anyway. A blanket over fresh seed is like a jacket for the soil, so the rain cannot knock it loose. Fences, basins and drain filters are nets that catch what already got away.
A.hint: Separate erosion control (keep soil in place) from sediment control (catch soil that moved).

steps.text: Erosion control measures protect the soil surface where it lies: seeding, mulch, erosion control blankets, slope roughening.
Sediment control measures trap soil after it is moving: silt fence, sediment traps and basins, inlet protection.
Only the seeded blanket acts on the slope surface before soil detaches, so it is the erosion control measure.

A.handbookFormula: \text{Erosion control: protect the surface (cover, vegetation). Sediment control: trap soil already moving.}
traps: Treating a silt fence as erosion control because it sits on the slope area
Choosing the biggest structure (the basin) instead of the one that acts at the source

B.statement: On a public school addition, the general contractor goes out of business after the drywall subcontractor has finished its work but before it has been paid. A mechanic's lien cannot be filed against public property. Which instrument gives the drywall subcontractor a way to recover the money it is owed?

choices.text: The bid bond the general contractor submitted with its proposal
The performance bond the general contractor furnished at award
The payment bond the general contractor furnished at award
The general contractor's commercial general liability policy

choiceNotes: A bid bond only protects the owner if the low bidder refuses to sign the contract. Its job ended at award.
A performance bond protects the owner: the surety finishes the work or pays to have it finished. It does not pay unpaid subcontractors.
Correct: a payment bond guarantees that the contractor's subcontractors and suppliers are paid. On public work it replaces the lien rights they cannot use.
Liability insurance covers injury and property damage to third parties, not unpaid contract balances.
B.eli5: Two bonds come with most public contracts. One promises the owner that the building gets finished. The other promises the workers and suppliers that they get paid. The drywall crew needs the second one.
B.hint: Ask who each bond protects: the owner, or the people who work for the contractor.

steps.text: A bid bond guarantees the low bidder will sign the contract and provide the other bonds. It does not cover the work itself.
A performance bond guarantees the owner that the work will be completed as the contract requires.
A payment bond guarantees payment to subcontractors, laborers and suppliers. Because liens are not allowed on public property, it is their protection on public jobs.

B.handbookFormula: \text{Bid bond: signs the contract; performance bond: owner gets the work; payment bond: subs and suppliers get paid}
traps: Choosing the performance bond because the contractor failed: it protects the owner's project, not the subcontractor's invoice
Thinking insurance covers money owed under a contract

B.statement: A county hires a construction manager as its agent (agency CM) for a new jail. Which statement correctly describes this delivery method?

choices.text: The CM holds the trade contracts and guarantees a maximum price for the work
The CM advises and manages for the county, which holds the trade contracts and the cost risk
The CM is also the designer of record, so the county signs one contract for design and construction
The CM is chosen by lowest bid after design is complete and performs most of the work itself

choiceNotes: Describes CM at risk: the CM signs the trade contracts and gives a guaranteed maximum price, so it carries cost risk.
Correct: an agency CM is a paid adviser. It manages schedule, cost and bidding for the owner, but the owner signs the trade contracts and keeps the cost risk.
Describes design-build, where one entity both designs and builds under a single contract.
Describes a general contractor under design-bid-build, selected by low bid on a finished design.
B.eli5: An agency CM is like hiring an experienced friend to run the project for you. The friend gives advice and keeps things moving, but you sign every contract and you pay if things cost more.
B.hint: The key word is agent. Who signs the trade contracts, and who pays if the price goes up?

steps.text: Agency CM: the construction manager acts as the owner's agent and is paid a fee for professional services.
The owner contracts directly with the trade contractors, so the owner carries the risk of cost overruns.
CM at risk differs exactly on that point: the CM holds the trade contracts and guarantees a maximum price.

B.handbookFormula: \text{Agency CM: adviser, owner holds contracts and risk; CM at risk: CM holds contracts, gives GMP}
traps: Mixing up agency CM and CM at risk: only the at-risk CM gives a guaranteed maximum price
Assuming any CM must also do the design

B.statement: A concrete pump on a bridge deck pour places 75 yd^3 per hour. Ready-mix trucks carry 9 yd^3 each, and one round trip (batching, travel to the site, discharge, washout and return) takes 80 min. The smallest number of trucks that keeps the pump supplied without a break is:
choiceNotes: Treats 80 min as 0.8 hr. 80 min is 1.33 hr, so each truck delivers far less per hour than this assumes.

Correct: each truck brings 9 yd^3 every 80 min, or 6.75 yd^3 per hour; 75 / 6.75 = 11.1, rounded up to 12 trucks.

B.statement: A contractor can use either of two hydraulic excavators to dig a basement in common earth that swells 25% from bank to loose. Excavator X produces 180 loose yd^3/hr at 100% efficiency and costs 140 dollars/hr to own and operate. Excavator Y produces 250 loose yd^3/hr at 100% efficiency and costs 210 dollars/hr. Either machine also needs one operator at 55 dollars/hr, and the job works 50 min per hour. Using the machine with the lower cost per bank cubic yard, that cost (dollars per bank yd^3) is most nearly:
choiceNotes: Multiplies by 1.25 instead of dividing, turning loose yards into more bank yards instead of fewer.

B.hint: Convert each machine to bank yards per working hour, and include the operator in the hourly cost.

B.statement: While a new subdivision street is being graded, a temporary roadside ditch on a 3% grade carries concentrated runoff. Which measure is most appropriate inside the ditch to slow the flow and trap sediment?

choices.text: A silt fence installed across the ditch bottom
Rock check dams placed across the ditch at intervals along its length
Loose straw mulch spread along the ditch bottom
A temporary sediment basin at the upstream end of the ditch

choiceNotes: Silt fence is for sheet flow at the toe of a slope. Across a ditch it is overtopped or undermined by concentrated flow and fails.
Correct: rock check dams are built for concentrated flow. Spacing them so each crest reaches the toe of the dam above turns the ditch into a series of slow pools.
Unanchored mulch washes away in channel flow; it is a surface cover for slopes, not a channel measure.
A sediment basin belongs at the downstream outlet where the runoff collects, not at the top of the ditch where little water has arrived yet.
B.eli5: Water running down a ditch is strong. A cloth fence gets knocked over or dug under. Small piles of rock across the ditch hold the water back in little steps, so it slows down and drops its dirt behind each pile.
B.hint: Sheet flow and concentrated flow need different measures. Which one is built for a channel?

steps.text: A ditch carries concentrated flow, so the measure must be one designed for channels.
Rock check dams slow channel flow and let sediment settle behind each dam.
They are spaced so the crest of each dam is at the elevation of the toe of the next dam upstream, so the water never speeds up between dams.

B.handbookFormula: \text{Check dam spacing: crest of downstream dam} = \text{toe of upstream dam}
traps: Using silt fence in concentrated flow
Putting a sediment basin where the water enters instead of where it leaves

B.statement: The activity-on-node network shown is for a storm sewer outfall, with all links finish-to-start and durations in days. The total float of Activity D (days) is:
choiceNotes: This is the free float of D (ES of F, 9, minus EF of D, 8), not the total float.
Correct: ES = 5 (after B), EF = 8; LF = earliest LS of successors = min(10, 12) = 10, LS = 7; total float = 7 - 5 = 2.
Takes the latest successor start (12) instead of the earliest in the backward pass: LF = 12, float = 4.
Computes LF - ES (10 - 5) and forgets to subtract the duration.
B.eli5: Find the longest chain through D: B (5 days), then D (3), then F and H (7) adds to 15 days. The whole job takes 17. So D can slip 2 days before it holds up the finish.
B.hint: Do the forward pass for the project length, then the backward pass taking the smallest late start of D's successors.

steps.text: Forward pass: A 0-3, B 0-5, C 3-9, D 5-8, E 5-12, F 9-14, G 12-15, H 15-17. The project takes 17 days.

Total float:

traps: Using the latest successor start in the backward pass

The overrun came from a one-time dewatering problem that is now solved, and the remaining work is expected to cost exactly what was budgeted for it. B.statement: A pipeline crew's three activities are linked as shown, where SS is start-to-start and FF is finish-to-finish, with lags and durations in days. Each activity runs without interruption once started, and there are no other constraints. The shortest time (days) from the start of trenching to the end of backfill is:
choiceNotes: Applies only the SS lags (B 2-8, C 3-8) and ends when trenching ends at day 10, ignoring both FF constraints.
Honors the FF lag on pipe laying (B ends day 11) but ignores the FF lag on backfill, letting C end with B.
Correct: B must end at least 1 day after A (day 11), so it runs 5-11; C must end at least 2 days after B, so it ends on day 13.
Treats every link as finish-to-start, adding the three durations end to end.
B.eli5: The pipe crew can start soon after the trench crew, but it cannot finish until a day after the trench is done. The backfill crew can also start early, but must finish two days after the pipe is in. Follow the finishes: trench ends day 10, pipe day 11, backfill day 13.
B.hint: For each activity, check both links: the SS link limits its start, the FF link limits its finish. The later one controls.

steps.text: Trenching: ES = 0, EF = 10.
Laying pipe: the SS link allows a start at day 2, but the FF link needs a finish no earlier than day 11, so with 6 days it starts on day 5.
Backfill: the SS link allows a start at day 6, but the FF link needs a finish no earlier than day 13.
Backfill finishes on day 13, and that is the duration of the work.

B.handbookFormula: \text{SS: start of B depends on start of A; FF: finish of B depends on finish of A}
traps: Checking only the SS lag and forgetting the FF lag that controls the finish
Treating overlapped activities as finish-to-start

B.statement: On the foundation plan, a cut line across a concrete wall ends in the callout shown. What does the callout tell the reader?

choices.text: Section 3 is drawn on sheet S-301, viewed in the direction the arrowheads point
Section 3 is drawn on sheet S-301, viewed opposite to the direction the arrowheads point
Section 301 is drawn on sheet 3, viewed in the direction the arrowheads point
Detail 3 is drawn on this sheet at a scale of 1:301, viewed from above

choiceNotes: Correct: the top of the bubble is the section number, the bottom is the sheet where it is drawn, and the arrowheads show which way the viewer looks.
Reverses the viewing direction. The arrowheads point the way the viewer looks at the cut.
Swaps the two halves of the bubble: the number on top identifies the section, the one below names the sheet.
Confuses the sheet reference with a scale, and a section is a cut view, not a plan view from above.
B.eli5: The bubble is an address. The top number is which drawing, the bottom is which page it is on. The little arrows show which way you would be looking if you sliced the wall there and stood beside the cut.
B.hint: A section callout is a cross-reference: what is on top, what is below, and what do the arrows show?

steps.text: The heavy dash-dot line is the cutting plane: where the wall is sliced.
In the bubble, the upper value identifies the section (3) and the lower value is the sheet where the section is drawn (S-301).
The solid arrowheads on the bubbles show the direction of view, here toward the right of the plan.

B.handbookFormula: \text{Section callout: section number over sheet number; arrowhead = direction of view}
